## The pipeline rewrites the column first {#sec-feature-pipeline}

![A machine-learning pipeline from data collection through feature transformation, selection, dimension reduction, and modelling, with model evaluation and tuning circled.](figures/sources/egu-feature-pipeline.png){fig-alt="Flow chart. Data collection and a feature database feed preparation, then feature extraction and transformation, feature selection, and dimension reduction, then modelling. Model evaluation and tuning is circled and feeds back." width="78%"}

[Hartmann and Rudolph](https://github.com/soga-lab/EGU2026_SC), EGU 2026 short course SC2.28, draw the usual order. The circled step is where the score is judged. A rewrite of the column that changes the mean shows up there as a number you cannot interpret. This hour is about that rewrite.

::: {.notes}
Trace the pipeline left to right and linger on the circled evaluation box. Ask what happens if a log or library-size normalisation is applied before the model is chosen—the metric still looks fine while the estimand changed. This slide sets the stake for everything that follows about transforms versus links.
:::
## The shape is often the scientific object {#sec-shape}

Environmental $Y$ is often:

- skewed, and strictly positive
- a count, or a composition
- full of zeros, or censored at a detection limit
- dependent in time or in space

A Gaussian `lm` can still be a useful approximation for a mean. It is a poor default when the support of $Y$ makes the approximation impossible. This hour follows [where we go deeper](#sec-deeper). Skew, in particular, is ordinary: [Quetilismus](#sec-quetilismus).

::: {.notes}
Read the bullet list as a checklist against CA-SYS and SPRUCE: counts, zeros, composition, dependence. The closing sentence is deliberately soft—a Gaussian mean can be fine—before the support argument bites. Link forward to Quetilismus as the cultural habit behind ignoring skew.
:::
## Quetilismus {#sec-quetilismus}

[Adrian Olszewski](https://www.2kmm.pl/blog/On-the-ubiquity-of-skewness-in-nature/) names the habit after Edgeworth's word for Quetelet. A unimodal curve is treated as a normal curve. Skew is then a defect to repair: drop the tails, wait for a larger sample, or transform until the histogram looks symmetric.

The [2KMM note of 15 May 2023](https://www.2kmm.pl/blog/On-the-ubiquity-of-skewness-in-nature/) and the PDF of that essay are the same text. The spelling-cleaned copy is the [Medium post of 2 January 2026](https://medium.com/@r.clin.res/on-the-ubiquity-of-skewness-in-nature-challenging-the-cult-of-the-gaussian-distribution-a1821dfe0f9a).

::: {.notes}
Name Quetilismus once, then list the three "repairs" Olszewski mocks: trim tails, wait for $n$, transform until symmetric. Students often recognise their own lab practice in the third. The duplicate URLs are for attribution only—do not read them aloud.
:::
## A product is not a sum

The classical central limit theorem is a statement about a **sum**, and it needs a finite variance. A product of positive steps is a different limit. Cascades, growth, and decay land on a log-normal, which is skewed. Cauchy, Lévy, and Pareto sit outside that classical sum.

Species abundance and environmental concentrations are on the product side ([Limpert, Stahel, and Abbt, 2001](https://doi.org/10.1641/0006-3568(2001)051[0341:LNDATS]2.0.CO;2); [Andersson, 2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-96010-6)). More rows do not turn a product into a sum.

::: {.notes}
Contrast sum versus product in one sentence each; Cauchy and Pareto are the "finite variance fails" examples. The carbon examples at the bottom are the punchline—bigger $n$ does not Gaussianise a multiplicative process. Ask whether read counts feel more like sums or products.
:::
## Skew is a description {#sec-skew-summary}

His summary, from the opening of the [Medium post](https://medium.com/@r.clin.res/on-the-ubiquity-of-skewness-in-nature-challenging-the-cult-of-the-gaussian-distribution-a1821dfe0f9a): a skewed description of a real process does not become less legitimate because the sample grew. Treating the normal law as the dominant description sets aside the mechanisms that generate the skew.

The next slide is the modelling consequence. The Gaussian assumption, when it is used, is about $Y \mid \mathbf{x}$, not about the raw histogram.

::: {.notes}
Quote the Medium opening idea: skew is not illegitimate because $n$ grew. Bridge to the next slide with the conditional phrase $Y \mid \mathbf{x}$. A common misread is to treat marginal skew as proof the linear model failed before any covariates are in the model.
:::
## The assumption is conditional

A QQ plot of the raw column $Y$ answers the wrong question.

The Gaussian linear model assumes that the **conditional** distribution $Y \mid \mathbf{x}$ is Gaussian, with constant variance. In residual form,

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2).
$$

Look at residuals, or at a residual QQ plot. Do not gate the analysis on a test of the marginal histogram.

::: {.notes}
Walk the displayed $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i$ and stress $\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$ as conditional on $\mathbf{x}$. The bold phrase "conditional distribution" is what students should underline. Raw-column QQ plots are the wrong object—say that twice.
:::
## How to read the plot :mag:

Points along the line support the reference shape. A curve, or a tail that leaves the line, is a departure. Illustrative residuals, seed 20261005.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
qq_gaussian <- bind_rows(
  tibble(model = "Gaussian lm, Gaussian Y", residual = resid(fit_lm_gauss)),
  tibble(model = "Gaussian lm, Poisson Y", residual = resid(fit_lm_count))
)
ggplot(qq_gaussian, aes(sample = residual)) +
  stat_qq_line() +
  stat_qq() +
  facet_wrap(~model)
```

::: {.notes}
This slide is code only; the figure is next. Point at `facet_wrap(~model)` and the two residual columns—Gaussian $Y$ versus Poisson $Y$ through the same `lm`. Ask which panel they expect to bend before you advance. Seed 20261005 is illustrative, not field data.
:::
## How to read the plot :mag: {#sec-qq-read}

![Two QQ plots. Left: residuals from a Gaussian response sit near the reference line. Right: residuals from a Gaussian linear model fitted to Poisson counts bend up in the right tail.](figures/generated/qq-gaussian-vs-count.png){fig-alt="QQ plots comparing Gaussian linear-model residuals when the response is Gaussian and when the response is a Poisson count." width="96%"}

::: {.notes}
Pair with the previous code slide: left panel is the sanity check, right panel is the misspecified count. Finger the right-tail lift as variance growing with the mean, not "non-normality" in the abstract. The preceding slide showed how those panels were produced.
:::
## The ends are allowed to wander

[Rodrigue](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/normality-tests-q-q-plots-natalie-rodrigue-qxlqc/): the horizontal axis is the quantile under the reference distribution. The vertical axis is the observed quantile. A straight line, with extra scatter at the ends, is the reference. Order statistics are noisier in the tails. A systematic curve is the departure. The named shapes are the [shape figures](#sec-qq-shapes).

::: {.notes}
Axes first: theoretical quantile horizontal, sample quantile vertical. Distinguish tail scatter (allowed) from a systematic bend (signal). Link to the four-shape figure before students memorise test names. Thirty seconds unless someone asks about order statistics.
:::
## A normality test is a poor gate

- with a large $n$, the test rejects a departure too small to change $\hat{\mu}$
- with a small $n$, it misses a departure large enough to matter
- the $p$-value does not say whether the **estimand** is distorted
- the test is aimed at the wrong object if you apply it to raw $Y$ rather than to the model you will trust

Prefer the QQ plot, and then a likelihood that matches $Y$. A formal test is a poor substitute for that plot.

::: {.notes}
Step through the four bullets; the third is the estimand point students miss. Large $n$ makes the fourth bullet bite—testing raw $Y$ when the model is conditional. Close with the QQ-plus-likelihood recipe on the slide.
:::
## Two sample sizes, two failures

Adrian Olszewski's rule, which this hour follows: stop using them, except when a reviewer demands the number. He counts more than 90 procedures.

- A small sample leaves them underpowered, so a real departure often passes.
- Past about 150–200 observations they reject almost any departure, including one too small to matter, while the central limit theorem for a **mean** is improving.
- Families aimed at skew, at kurtosis, and at the whole distribution contradict one another. Shapiro–Wilk is one of those families, not a universal test.

::: {.notes}
Give Olszewski's "stop using them" line, then the 150–200 observation remark and the small-sample underpowering bullet. "More than 90 procedures" is rhetorical scale—do not treat it as a number to defend. Shapiro–Wilk is one family among many contradictory ones.
:::
## The same sample, opposite answers

![A normal QQ plot with a step, two histograms of the same sample, and a table of normality-test p-values that disagree.](figures/sources/qq-versus-normality-tests.png){fig-alt="For a sample of 400 with skewness near zero and kurtosis near 3, the QQ plot steps in the middle and the histogram has two modes. Shapiro–Wilk gives 0.123. Several moment tests do not flag the sample. Lilliefors, Cramér–von Mises, and Anderson–Darling do." width="92%"}

$n = 400$, skewness about 0, kurtosis about 3. Shapiro–Wilk gives $p = 0.123$. Lilliefors, Cramér–von Mises, and Anderson–Darling reject. The QQ plot shows the step either way.

::: {.notes}
Restate $n=400$ and the step in the QQ plot before reading any $p$-values. Shapiro–Wilk 0.123 versus rejecting Lilliefors/AD is the lesson—tests disagree while the plot stays honest. Ask which diagnostic they would trust for choosing a family.
:::
## Four shapes on the QQ plot {#sec-qq-shapes}

![Four normal QQ plots: Gaussian points on the line, heavy tails as an S-curve, right skew as a concave-up bend, light tails as a flat S.](figures/sources/qq-four-shapes.png){fig-alt="Four QQ plots against a normal reference. Gaussian points follow the line. Heavy tails flare at both ends. Right skew bends concave-up. Light tails make a flatter S." width="96%"}

Ends that flare are heavy tails. A concave-up bend is right skew. A concave-down bend is left skew. A flat S is light tails. The shaded ribbon on the Gaussian panel is a generic band. The band to use is the [tail-sensitive one](#sec-qq-band).

::: {.notes}
Point at each panel in the four-shape figure while naming flare, concave-up, concave-down, flat S. The generic ribbon on the Gaussian panel is not the tail-sensitive band—preview the `bandType = "ts"` slide. Students confuse heavy tails with right skew; keep the vocabulary separate.
:::
## Jumps, steps, and stray points

[Rodrigue](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/normality-tests-q-q-plots-natalie-rodrigue-qxlqc/) names three patterns that are not a smooth curve.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} A jump or a gap: two groups pooled, or a rounding artefact.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} A staircase: a discrete or heavily rounded response. The residuals keep that discreteness.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} One or two points off an otherwise straight line: outliers. Check whether they move the fit before deleting them.

Below about 30 observations, even a Gaussian sample wiggles. Do not read that noise as a new shape.

::: {.notes}
Step the three fragments: pooled groups, discrete $Y$, outliers. The $n<30$ rule is on the slide—use it to stop over-interpretation. Ask which pattern they have seen in sequencing residuals (often staircase or stray points).
:::
## The straight line is the Gaussian case

![A grid of QQ plots and histograms for Gaussian, beta, uniform, skewed, bimodal, truncated, discrete, and outlier samples.](figures/sources/qq-distribution-gallery.png){fig-alt="Sixteen distributions. Each row shows a normal QQ plot and the matching histogram. Only the Gaussian row follows the reference line. Skew bends the plot, bimodality steps it, and heavy tails flare the ends." width="96%"}

Click the figure. Each distribution is a QQ plot against a normal reference, then the histogram. Only the Gaussian row stays on the line. The others are the shapes from the previous slide, including discrete samples and a sample with outliers.

::: {.notes}
Lightbox the gallery if time allows; otherwise name beta, uniform, bimodal, discrete rows. Only the Gaussian row tracks the line—everything else reuses the vocabulary from the four-shape slide. About one minute with the clickable figure.
:::
## A tail-sensitive band {#sec-qq-band}

The ribbon to draw is the simultaneous tail-sensitive band of [Aldor-Noiman and colleagues (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2013.847865). In [`qqplotr`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=qqplotr) that is `bandType = "ts"`. It is implemented for a **normal** QQ plot. A pointwise ribbon is a different object.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
ggplot(residuals, aes(sample = residual)) +
  qqplotr::stat_qq_band(bandType = "ts") +
  qqplotr::stat_qq_line() +
  qqplotr::stat_qq_point()
```

Points outside that band are the departure. A $p$-value from a normality test is not a summary of the same picture. The workshop residuals are the [two QQ plots](#sec-qq-read) above, read this way.

::: {.notes}
Highlight `bandType = "ts"` in the code chunk—normal QQ only. Contrast simultaneous tail-sensitive band with a pointwise ribbon. Tie back to the generated Gaussian-versus-count residuals once students see points outside the band.
:::
## Three means, three questions {#sec-three-means}

![Table of the arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic means, with formulas and the inequality A at least G at least H.](figures/sources/arithmetic-geometric-harmonic.jpeg){fig-alt="Three columns. Arithmetic mean is a sum divided by n. Geometric mean is the n-th root of a product. Harmonic mean is the reciprocal of the mean of reciprocals. For positive numbers, A is at least G, which is at least H." width="78%"}

[Sharmi Murali](https://medium.com/@sharmi.v.murali/arithmetic-mean-vs-geometric-mean-vs-harmonic-mean-b956cf1b2b3f): a sum, a product, or a reciprocal. $A \ge G \ge H$ for positive numbers, with equality only when every value is the same. A product process wants $G$, and logging $Y$ [changes the estimand](#sec-log-estimand) to that mean.

::: {.notes}
Walk the three columns in the figure: sum, product, reciprocal. $A \ge G \ge H$ is the inequality to remember. Link logging $Y$ to the geometric mean and forward to the log-estimand slide—students often report $A$ after a log transform.
:::
## A box plot hides the shape

A box plot reports a median, a box, and whiskers. It does not show a second mode, a pile of ties, or how many points sit in the tail. [The case against using it alone](https://medium.com/data-science/why-a-box-plot-should-not-be-used-alone-and-some-plots-to-use-it-with-23381f7e3cb6) is that those are often the features a carbon response actually has.

Prefer a plot that keeps the raw points. A raincloud adds a density and a short summary beside them ([Scherer, 6 June 2021](https://www.cedricscherer.com/2021/06/06/visualizing-distributions-with-raincloud-plots-and-how-to-create-them-with-ggplot2/)).

::: {.notes}
List what a box plot hides: bimodality, ties, tail mass. Carbon responses often have those features. Raincloud is the constructive alternative named on the slide—density plus points plus a small summary.
:::
## Show the difference, not a star {#sec-gardner-altman}

![Five panels from Ho and colleagues: a bar chart, a box plot, a scatter with means, a null distribution of the difference, and a Gardner–Altman plot of the mean difference with an interval.](figures/sources/gardner-altman-figure-1.png){fig-alt="Figure 1 of Ho and colleagues. Panels a to c summarise two groups. Panel d shows a permutation null for the mean difference and a p-value. Panel e shows the mean difference, its bootstrap distribution, and a 95 percent interval on a difference axis." width="86%"}

[Ho and colleagues](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-019-0470-3). Panel e is the graphic this workshop keeps: $\Delta$ and an interval.

::: {.notes}
Scan panels a–c as what not to stop at, then land on panel e: mean difference $\Delta$ with an interval on a difference axis. Contrast with a lone star or $p$-value. This is the reporting standard the pitfalls section keeps returning to.
:::
## Four questions, not one test {#sec-four-comparisons}

![Four cards: tests of whole distributions, stochastic superiority, specific features such as quantiles, and parametric parameters.](figures/sources/four-kinds-of-comparison.jpeg){fig-alt="Four panels. Whole empirical distributions ask whether two distribution functions are equal. Stochastic superiority asks whether one sample tends to be larger. Quantiles and scales ask about a named feature. Parametric tests ask about a parameter of a named distribution." width="88%"}

[Olszewski](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/adrianolszewski_there-exist-900-statistical-tests-many-share-7479152921432018944-tEK7/) groups comparisons of two or more samples by the question, from the most general to the most specific. About nine hundred named procedures sit in these groups. The name of the procedure is not the hypothesis.

::: {.notes}
Read the four cards left to right as increasing specificity. "Nine hundred" is Olszewski's scale—use it to deflate test shopping. Ask which card a Mann–Whitney user actually picked (often not the one they think).
:::
## Whole distributions, then the tails

A test of the empirical distribution functions asks only whether $F = G$. It does not say whether the difference is a shift, a scale, or a shape.

[Olszewski's family](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7413639530941091841/): Kolmogorov–Smirnov uses the largest vertical gap, and it is the least sensitive of the three. Cramér–von Mises integrates the squared gap, so a small gap that persists can count. Anderson–Darling uses the same integral with extra weight in the tails. For a heavy-tailed flux, Anderson–Darling is the one that looks where the mass of the question sits.

::: {.notes}
$F=G$ is the whole-distribution null—no location story yet. Compare KS (max gap), CvM (integrated gap), AD (tail-weighted). For heavy-tailed flux, name Anderson–Darling as the tail-aware member of the trio on the slide.
:::
## A rank test is not a mean test

![Two examples. Left: equal medians, Mann–Whitney p below 0.001, and about 70 percent stochastic superiority. Right: medians differ by 10, Mann–Whitney p above 0.999, and stochastic superiority of 50 percent.](figures/sources/mann-whitney-not-a-median-test.jpeg){fig-alt="Left panel: two samples with the same median and Mann–Whitney p below 0.001, with about 70 percent of pairs ordered one way. Right panel: medians differ by 10, Mann–Whitney p above 0.999, and stochastic superiority of one half." width="78%"}

Mann–Whitney estimates $P(B>A)+\tfrac12 P(B=A)$. Equal medians can be decisive. A gap of 10 can be invisible. For a median, use [quantile regression](https://gist.github.com/adrianolszewski/2cec75678e1183e4703589bfd22fa8b2).

::: {.notes}
Left panel: equal medians, $p<0.001$, ~70% stochastic superiority. Right panel: medians differ by 10, $p>0.999$, 50% superiority. Read those numbers off the figure before defining the estimand. Mann–Whitney is not a median test—quantile regression is named for a median question.
:::
## Ranks answer a different question

Unless the two distributions differ only by a shift, a rank test mixes location, scale, and shape. Mann–Whitney can be small when the means are equal and the variances are not, and large when the means differ and the variances differ the other way. That is Studentization: the null of a rank test is not the null of a mean.

If the planned question is a mean, stay with a procedure for a mean: a permutation Welch test, Freedman–Lane, or a wild bootstrap. Brunner–Munzel is the rank procedure that allows unequal variances, and it still estimates a probability, not $\mu$. The map of those choices is [the six columns](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/adrianolszewski_there-exist-900-statistical-tests-many-share-7479152921432018944-tEK7/).

::: {.notes}
Studentization is the keyword: rank null mixes location, scale, and shape. If the estimand is $\mu$, list permutation Welch, Freedman–Lane, wild bootstrap from the slide. Brunner–Munzel still targets a probability. Point to the six-column map link as the decision chart.
:::
## Six routes, one of them a mean

![Six columns of nonparametric comparisons: whole distributions, stochastic superiority, generalised locations, quantiles, robust mean-like estimators, and arithmetic means.](figures/sources/nonparametric-comparison-map.png){fig-alt="A diagram with six columns, from tests of the whole distribution, through ranks and quantiles, to permutation tests of an arithmetic mean." width="92%"}

The columns are questions. Mann–Whitney is the second, not a median. The last column is still a mean: permutation Welch, Freedman–Lane, a wild bootstrap.

::: {.notes}
Gesture across the six columns of the map image. Mann–Whitney lives in stochastic superiority, not the mean column. The last column is where permutation Welch and friends sit—keep that column in mind for the next slides.
:::
## Keep the mean, and change the standard error

![Table of ways to compare two means when variances differ, when there are outliers, or when the distribution is not Gaussian.](figures/sources/compare-means-no-covariate.png){fig-alt="A table. Equal variances: the ordinary t-test. Unequal variances: Welch. Outliers: Yuen or a robust regression, which changes the estimand to a trimmed or weighted mean. Non-Gaussian: a permutation or bootstrap t-test." width="86%"}

[Olszewski](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity/7445521856679407619/) keeps the mean when that is the question. Welch does not need a pretest of the variances. Yuen changes the target to a trimmed mean. A permutation Welch test keeps the mean when the distribution is not Gaussian.

::: {.notes}
Read the table row by row: equal variances → ordinary $t$; unequal → Welch without an $F$ pretest; outliers → Yuen and a new estimand. The bottom row is permutation or bootstrap $t$ when the mean stays the question. Yuen is the row where the estimand quietly changes.
:::
## The same mean, with a covariate

![The lower half of the same table: ANCOVA by ordinary least squares, sandwich standard errors, generalised least squares, Freedman–Lane, and a wild bootstrap.](figures/sources/compare-means-with-covariate.png){fig-alt="Rows for a covariate-adjusted comparison of two means. Ordinary least squares when variances match and slopes are parallel. Sandwich standard errors or generalised least squares when variances differ. Freedman–Lane or a wild bootstrap when the distribution is not Gaussian." width="96%"}

Adding a covariate does not force a rank test. Ordinary least squares is the ANCOVA when the variances match and the slopes are parallel. Unequal variances move the standard error to a sandwich estimator or to generalised least squares. A non-Gaussian residual moves the test to Freedman–Lane, or to a wild bootstrap, still for the mean.

::: {.notes}
This is the lower half of Olszewski's table—pair it mentally with the previous slide. ANCOVA by OLS needs parallel slopes and equal variance; sandwich or GLS relax variance; Freedman–Lane or wild bootstrap relax Gaussian residuals. The estimand remains a mean difference adjusted for the covariate.
:::
## Prefer Welch when the model is this simple

![Side-by-side equivalence of a pooled t-test with ordinary least squares, and a Welch test with generalised least squares and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.](figures/sources/welch-versus-ols-1.png){fig-alt="Two blocks. A pooled t-test matches a Wald test from ordinary least squares, estimate minus 2.99, p 0.049. A Welch test matches generalised least squares with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, the same estimate, p 0.052." width="72%"}

Start from Welch ([Olszewski](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7400680154634686464/)). The pooled test forces a common variance. In his sketch the estimate is $-2.99$ either way; the $p$-values are 0.049 and 0.052.

::: {.notes}
Same estimate $-2.99$, different $p$: 0.049 pooled versus 0.052 Welch. Use that pair to show the decision is in the standard error, not the contrast. Pooled $t$ equals homoscedastic OLS; Welch equals GLS with Satterthwaite df on the figure.
:::
## A permutation $p$ for the same Welch statistic {#sec-perm-welch}

[Olszewski](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7490552621573922816/): `MKinfer::perm.t.test` uses the Welch–Satterthwaite statistic unless you set `var.equal = TRUE`. Leave the default. Do not pretest the variances with an $F$ test.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
result <- MKinfer::perm.t.test(
  response ~ group, data = data, permStat = TRUE
)
MKinfer::h0plot(result)
```

::: {.notes}
The call returns the classical $p$ and the permutation $p$. Compare them, and look at the null distribution of the permuted statistic as well as the residual QQ plot. Use more than 9999 draws for a stable $p$, and on the order of 50,000 if the level of interest is below 0.001. Record the seed. Permuting the raw difference of means quietly assumes equal variances. The studentized statistic is the one Janssen (1997) gives for unequal variances; he lists that paper under the post. A reported permutation $p$ of exactly 0 is a convention about the draws, not a probability.
:::

## Compare the two $p$-values, then the null plot

`h0plot()` on the same object shows the permuted statistic under the null beside the two $p$-values on the printout. If the classical and permutation $p$ disagree, the Gaussian approximation was doing work.

::: {.notes}
This slide is only the picture. The draw count, seed, and Welch-versus-raw permutation point are on the previous slide's notes. Thirty seconds.
:::

## A bell curve is not a feature test {#sec-meaningless-sigma}

![Recovery rates piled against 100 percent, with a 1-sigma interval of 92 plus or minus 12 and a 2-sigma interval of 92 plus or minus 24, beside a normal bell marked 68, 95, and 99.7 percent.](figures/sources/egu-recovery-two-sigma.png){fig-alt="Histogram of percent area recovered within 30 years, piled at 100 percent. A 1-sigma band of 92 plus or minus 12 stays inside 0 to 100. A 2-sigma band of 92 plus or minus 24 does not. A Gaussian bell sits beside the histogram." width="92%"}

[Hartmann and Rudolph](https://github.com/soga-lab/EGU2026_SC). The 2-sigma interval is 92 ± 24%, so it leaves 0–100. The bell beside it is the 68%, 95%, 99.7% picture. A normality test does not turn that interval into a recovery rate. The same objection applies to a concentration, a count, or a composition.

::: {.notes}
Point at the histogram piled at 100% and the 92 ± 24% band leaving the 0–100 scale. The bell's 68/95/99.7 labels are the wrong feature for bounded recovery. A normality test on such data does not repair the interval—shape and support are separate failures.
:::
## The excuse is not a diagnosis

The same slides list the defences of that summary:

- everybody reports it this way
- the variance was large
- \(n\) was too small for anything more accurate
- it is the reporting standard
- one only wanted the mean and the variability
- the statistically careful version made the story disappear

None of these is a reason to attach a Gaussian spread to a feature whose scale forbids it. The [QQ plot](#sec-qq-read) shows the shape. It does not choose the summary.

::: {.notes}
Read two or three excuses from the bullet list and invite the room to name others they have heard. Close with the QQ plot link: diagnosis of shape is not the same as choosing a summary on the right scale. Keep the tone practical, not preachy.
:::
## Before you transform $Y$

Write two answers, and keep them.

1. Why is transforming the response usually a bad default?
2. What do you do instead when a Gaussian model for $Y$ does not fit?

[Olszewski's](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/why-transforming-response-regression-analysis-testing-olszewski/) answers, from the 2022 note, follow the variance-stabilising case. A multiplicative process is the case he keeps. A skewed histogram is not.

::: {.notes}
Pause on the two numbered questions—let someone answer before you advance. Olszewski's "bad default" is about rewriting the estimand without science; the alternative is a model matched to $Y$. Skew alone is not on his justification list.
:::
## A transformation can be the right scale

A transform is justified when it matches the science:

- a multiplicative effect, so that logs are the natural contrast
- a variance that grows with the mean, and a log that stabilises it
- a physical rate that is already defined on a log scale

It is not justified by "the histogram looked skewed" alone. What that shortcut costs starts at [a transform rewrites the question](#sec-transform-rewrite).

::: {.notes}
Walk the three justified bullets: multiplicative effects, variance growing with mean, physical log scale. The closing sentence is the guardrail—histogram skew is not on the list. Link to the transform-rewrite slide for the cost of ignoring that guardrail.
:::
## Match the transform to $v(\mu)$ {#sec-vst}

[Huber, chapter 13](https://www.huber.embl.de/msmb/13-chap.html#mean-variance-relationships-and-variance-stabilizing-transformations), writes $v(\mu)$ for the way the variance trends with the mean. Three prototypes cover most assays:

- constant: $v(\mu) = c$
- Poisson-like: $v(\mu) = a\mu$
- quadratic: the standard deviation proportional to the mean, so $v(\mu) = b\mu^2$

A real measurement can add them. For microarray fluorescence he cites Rocke and Durbin (2001): background plus a multiplicative noise, $v(\mu) = b\mu^2 + c$. A variance-stabilising transformation is built from that curve, so replicate spread no longer tracks the mean. One power for the whole sample, as on the [Yeo–Johnson slide](#sec-yeo), does not use $v(\mu)$.

::: {.notes}
Huber's three prototypes—constant, Poisson-like $a\mu$, quadratic $b\mu^2$—are the vocabulary. Rocke–Durbin adds $b\mu^2+c$ as a realistic assay. Contrast VST built from $v(\mu)$ with Yeo–Johnson chasing a bell shape for the whole column.
:::
## A VST is for a Euclidean next step {#sec-vst-pca}

Reasons for analysing the transformed scale:

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} a plot, or a heatmap, that spends its ink across the range

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} PCA, or a clustering that uses correlation, no longer dominated by a few very large means

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} a method that assumes identical, homoskedastic noise

That is the machine-learning case: a method whose geometry is Euclidean and wants a roughly constant spread. The transformation is still a new response. Inference for $\mu$ on the original support stays with the [link](#sec-glm-versus-transform).

::: {.notes}
Step the three fragments: heatmaps, PCA dominated by large means, homoskedastic noise for ML. VST is a preprocessing choice for geometry, not automatic inference on the original scale. The link at the end points to GLMs as the inference path.
:::
## A transform rewrites the question {#sec-transform-rewrite}

A logarithm changes a difference of arithmetic means into a ratio of geometric means. A Box–Cox power such as $-0.67$ is not a unit anyone measured.

On $\log Y$ against $x$, a small coefficient is nearly a percentage: $\exp(0.05) \approx 1.05$. A coefficient of $0.5$ is not a 50% change, because $\exp(0.5) \approx 1.65$. The inequality that separates the two means is [written later](#sec-log-estimand).

::: {.notes}
Box–Cox power $-0.67$ is the absurd unit example. Contrast $\exp(0.05)\approx 1.05$ with $\exp(0.5)\approx 1.65$ so students stop saying "0.5 on the log is 50%". Forward to the log-estimand inequality slide.
:::
## The variance travels with the mean

In a Gaussian model the mean and the variance are separate parameters. After a log they are tied: a log-normal variance depends on the mean. A power chosen only to stabilise the spread changes that relationship even when the power is not a logarithm.

::: {.notes}
Gaussian $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ separate; log-normal ties them. Any power transform for stabilisation also couples mean and spread—even when it is not $\log$. One sentence slide: do not rush.
:::
## The interval does not travel back

$$
g\{\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)\} \ne \mathbb{E}\{g(Y) \mid x\}
$$

unless $g$ is linear. A confidence interval, a moment, or a test computed on $g(Y)$ is not the same object on the original scale after you apply $g^{-1}$. A $p$-value on the transformed response and an interval on the original scale can disagree about the claim. The log case is the [estimand slide](#sec-log-estimand).

::: {.notes}
Read the displayed inequality once; Jensen is the name students may know. Emphasise that $g^{-1}$ of a CI on $g(Y)$ is not a CI for $\mathbb{E}(Y)$. The log-estimand slide makes the arithmetic mean versus geometric mean concrete.
:::
## A logarithm needs a positive response

$\log Y$ is undefined when $Y$ can be negative. Adding a constant, as in $\log(Y + c)$, defines a different response. A bone-density T-score is one measurement that is allowed to be negative. Quantile regression does not need the sign. Yeo–Johnson is the power that allows negatives, and the [later slide](#sec-yeo) says what that power costs.

::: {.notes}
$\log(Y+c)$ is a new response, not a fix for negatives. T-score is the named example of legitimate negative $Y$. Quantile regression and Yeo–Johnson are the two exits named on the slide—different estimands, different costs.
:::
## The pooled histogram is the wrong picture

Conditional Gaussian groups with different means look skewed once you pool them. In his sketch the groups are normal, seed 1000, and the model is `lm(DV ~ IV)`. Logging the pooled $Y$ because the histogram is skewed spoils residuals that were already close to Gaussian.

Transform when the **conditional** distribution is skewed. That is what the residual plot checks. If $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$ is already approximately Gaussian, the transform is not the remedy.

::: {.notes}
Olszewski's sketch: normal groups, different means, pooled skew. Logging pooled $Y$ can wreck residuals that were fine conditional on `IV`. Seed 1000 and `lm(DV ~ IV)` are on the slide—illustrative. Conditional versus marginal is the whole point.
:::
## The centre has to match the scale {#sec-scales}

```{r}
#| echo: false
math <- function(tex) gt::html(sprintf('<span class="math inline">\\(%s\\)</span>', tex))

scales <- data.frame(
  Scale = c(
    "Binomial", "Nominal", "Ordinal", "Interval",
    "Rational", "Logistic", "Concentration"
  ),
  Measure = I(c(
    "Success or failure",
    "Category membership",
    math("\\text{ordered by } <"),
    math("d=|x_1-x_2|"),
    math("x_1/x_2"),
    math("(x-l)/(u-x)"),
    "Part of a constant sum"
  )),
  Example = c(
    "Rainy days", "Soil types", "Hurricane category",
    "Time, location", "Length, weight, isotope ratio",
    "Elevation, depth", "TOC, recovery rate"
  ),
  Similarity = c(
    "Equality only", "Equality", "Rank order",
    "Additive, near 0", "Multiplicative, near 1",
    "Log-ratio", "Aitchison distance"
  ),
  Centre = I(c(
    math("np"),
    math("\\text{mode, }\\bar{x}_{\\mathrm{geo}},\\, np_i"),
    math("Q_{50}"),
    "Arithmetic mean",
    "Geometric mean",
    "Logistic mean",
    "Geometric mean"
  )),
  Spread = I(c(
    math("np(1-p)"),
    "Entropy",
    math("Q_{75}-Q_{25}"),
    "Arithmetic sd",
    "Geometric sd",
    "Logistic variance",
    "Compositional variance"
  )),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

scales |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_options(
    table.font.size = "15px",
    data_row.padding = gt::px(2),
    column_labels.font.size = "15px"
  )
```

[Hartmann and Rudolph](https://github.com/soga-lab/EGU2026_SC). An arithmetic mean is the interval row. A ratio wants a geometric mean. TOC and a recovery are parts of a sum, not interval measurements.

::: {.notes}
Walk the gt table row by row: Interval → arithmetic mean; Rational → geometric; Concentration → geometric on parts of a sum. Hartmann and Rudolph's TOC and recovery examples are compositional, not interval. Ask which centre matches an isotope ratio versus a recovery rate.
:::
## A constant sum is a simplex

If the parts add to a constant, the point is not free in the plane. The picture: \(x + y = 1\) is a line segment, not a square. A sequencing library is the same constraint. The counts in one sample add to the library size, so a gene is a share of that sum. A Gaussian interval on the count, or on a shifted logarithm of the count, does not respect it.

::: {.notes}
Use $x+y=1$ as the line-segment picture before sequencing. Library size fixes the sum of counts; a gene share lives on a simplex. Gaussian intervals on raw counts ignore that constraint—preview compositional methods without opening the full chapter.
:::
## Five steps that rewrite \(Y\)

For a positive \(x\), a common checklist is:

- inspect a histogram, a box plot, or a QQ plot
- if the lower limit is positive, add a constant
- take \(\log x\) and check that the logs look more Gaussian
- average the logs and take their standard deviation
- exponentiate both, and report the geometric mean times or divided by the geometric standard deviation

They note that this interval stays positive. That is not the same as an interval for \(\mathbb{E}(Y)\).

::: {.notes}
Read the five-step checklist aloud once. The slide's own caveat is the punchline: positivity of the reported interval is not an interval for $\mathbb{E}(Y)$. Students recognise this pipeline from papers; name what estimand the geometric mean times/divided by GSD actually targets.
:::
## The exponential does not return the moment

\(\exp(\overline{\log x})\) is the geometric mean. It is not \(\mathbb{E}(Y)\). Exponentiating the standard deviation of the logs does not return the standard deviation of \(Y\). A shift before the logarithm is a third response. The [inequality](#sec-log-estimand) is why the two means differ. Prefer a model for \(\mu\), or a robust summary, over this sequence.

::: {.notes}
$\exp(\overline{\log x})$ is the geometric mean, not $\mathbb{E}(Y)$. Exponentiating the log SD is not the SD on the original scale. Shift before log is a third response—link to the log-estimand inequality slide.
:::
## A logit link stays inside the bounds

For a recovery, or any proportion, model \(\operatorname{logit}(\pi)\) with \(\pi = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)\). When \(Y\) is binary this is logistic regression. The same link is the model for a proportion. The reported interval is the inverse logit of the interval for the linear predictor. It stays in \((0, 1)\), and the test is a test of \(\pi\).

It is not the arithmetic mean of a column that was transformed until a QQ plot looked straight.

::: {.notes}
Model $\operatorname{logit}(\pi)$ with $\pi=\mathbb{E}(Y\mid x)$; inverse logit intervals stay in $(0,1)$. Contrast with transforming a column until a QQ plot looks straight—that is not a test of $\pi$. Binary and proportion cases share the same link sentence on the slide.
:::
## Put the curve in $\mu$, not in $Y$

A nonlinear regression lets $\mu$ be a nonlinear function of $x$. A generalised linear model leaves $Y$ alone and puts a link on $\mu$. Both keep the original response. The link is the rest of this hour, from the [skeleton](#sec-skeleton).

::: {.notes}
Nonlinear regression bends $\mu(x)$; GLM bends $g(\mu)$ while $Y$ stays on its support. Both keep the measured response. Point to the skeleton slide as the next hour's route map.
:::
## Or model the variance, or change the summary

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} [Generalised least squares or estimating equations](#sec-ols-replacements) when the variance or the correlation is the problem, and the mean is still the target.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} Quantile regression when the target is a quantile, including a median, and including censored $Y$.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} A robust or rank procedure when the question is not an arithmetic mean. The [map](#sec-four-comparisons) is that choice. A [permutation Welch test](#sec-perm-welch) is the choice when the mean remains the question.

::: {.notes}
Step the three fragments: GLS/GEE for variance structure; quantile regression for a quantile estimand; robust/rank or permutation Welch when the mean is not the question. The four-comparisons map is the routing table for fragment three.
:::
## $\log Y$ changes the estimand {#sec-log-estimand}

A Gaussian model for $\log Y$ targets $\mathbb{E}(\log Y \mid x)$.

$$
\exp\{\mathbb{E}(\log Y \mid x)\} \le \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x),
$$

with equality only in degenerate cases. The left-hand side behaves like a geometric mean. The right-hand side is the arithmetic mean on the original scale.

$\log(Y+1)$ is a third response. Zeros were the reason for the $+1$, and they are still in the model, only hidden.

For counts, start from a distribution on the non-negative integers ([O'Hara and Kotze, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2041-210X.2010.00021.x); [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015]).

::: {.notes}
Read the inequality: $\exp\{\mathbb{E}(\log Y\mid x)\}\le \mathbb{E}(Y\mid x)$. $\log(Y+1)$ hides zeros but changes the response again. Close with counts needing an integer model—O'Hara and Kotze on the slide.
:::
## Powers that chase a Gaussian shape {#sec-yeo}

Yeo–Johnson chooses a power, including for zeros and negative values, so that the transformed sample is closer to Gaussian. When the next method is Euclidean, such as a PCA, the transform that follows $v(\mu)$ is the [variance-stabilising transformation](#sec-vst).

- the criterion is closeness to a bell shape, not a scientific unit
- the inverse transform is awkward, so a mean on the transformed scale is hard to say in the original unit
- if you use it, describe the original $Y$ with the median and the quartiles

It does not replace a likelihood whose support is the support of $Y$.

::: {.notes}
Yeo–Johnson optimises toward Gaussianity for PCA-like steps, not toward a scientific unit. If used, report median and quartiles on original $Y$. VST from $v(\mu)$ is the principled alternative named in the first bullet's cross-link.
:::
## A test is a model with one factor {#sec-tests-as-linear}

[Lindeløv](https://lindeloev.github.io/tests-as-linear/) writes the common tests as linear models. A Pearson correlation is the slope in `lm(scale(y) ~ scale(x))`: standardising both variables makes that slope equal to $r$. A $\chi^2$ test of counts is a Poisson log-linear model, `glm(counts ~ group, family = poisson)`, compared with an intercept-only model.

The model is the more flexible object. It keeps the same contrast and adds a covariate, a variance weight, or a link. A named test usually cannot.

::: {.notes}
Pearson $r$ as `lm(scale(y)~scale(x))` and $\chi^2$ as Poisson `glm(counts~group)` are the two Lindeløv examples. The model generalises with covariates, weights, and links; the named test often does not.
:::
## A paired $t$ reports the mean

[Loïc](https://statsxomics.blog/2024/05/25/why-you-should-use-regression-models-instead-of-tests-for-statistical-inferences/), seed 1234, 100 people measured twice. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test gives $V = 1711$ and $p = 0.005$. The paired $t$ test gives a mean difference of $-0.42$, an interval from $-0.69$ to $-0.14$, and $p = 0.003$. The sign is the order of the two levels.

Both reject. Only the paired $t$ test says how large the mean change is. The signed-rank test is a statement about the ranks of the within-person differences.

::: {.notes}
Wilcoxon $V=1711$, $p=0.005$ versus paired $t$ mean difference $-0.42$ with interval $-0.69$ to $-0.14$, $p=0.003$, seed 1234. Both reject; only the $t$ states how large the mean shift is. Signed-rank is about ranks of within-person differences.
:::
## The pair is a random intercept

An ordinary `lm` on the same rows, without the person, keeps the estimate at $0.42$ and inflates the standard error to $0.28$, so $p = 0.14$. A random intercept, `(1 | ind)`, keeps $0.42$ and brings the standard error back to $0.14$. The $t$ statistic returns to $2.99$, the paired test.

In that fit the person-level variance is $3.06$ and the residual variance is $0.96$. Dropping the pair does not change the estimate. It charges the within-person contrast with the between-person noise.

::: {.notes}
Naive `lm` inflates SE to $0.28$, $p=0.14$; `(1|ind)` returns SE $0.14$ and $t=2.99$. Person variance $3.06$ versus residual $0.96$ on the slide. Dropping the pairing does not move the $0.42$ estimate—it adds between-person noise to the wrong error.
:::
## When ordinary least squares is the wrong skeleton {#sec-ols-replacements}

If the Gaussian, independent, constant-variance assumptions fail, the replacements are still models.

- Generalised least squares: a known pattern for the variance, which is the Welch test when the pattern is a group.
- Generalised estimating equations: a working correlation and a sandwich standard error.
- A generalised linear model: a distribution for $Y$ and a link for $\mu$.
- A generalised additive model: a smooth function of $x$ in place of a straight line.

This hour then stays with the generalised linear model. The others are named so a later choice is a choice of estimand, not a new religion.

::: {.notes}
Four bullets: GLS, GEE, GLM, GAM—each names what breaks in OLS. This hour stays on GLM; the list prevents swapping religion when the estimand should change. Welch as GLS for group variance is the bridge back to earlier slides.
:::
## `aov()` is Type I {#sec-anova-type}

![A warning that aov() in R is Type I ANOVA, so the test of treatment depends on whether baseline or treatment is entered first.](figures/sources/ancova-type-i-order.jpeg){fig-alt="Four rows. lm, car::Anova with type 2, and permuco are marked safe. aov is marked not safe, because the order of baseline and treatment changes the sums of squares." width="78%"}

[Olszewski](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7444337265641684992/): `aov()` is Type I, so the treatment $F$ in his sketch is 16.6 or 38.7 depending on order. `car::Anova(type = 2)` does not inherit that order.

::: {.notes}
Treatment $F$ is 16.6 or 38.7 depending on entry order in Olszewski's sketch. `car::Anova(type=2)` is marked safe on the figure. Ask what happens if baseline and treatment are swapped in `aov()`.
:::
## Three types, then a deviance {#sec-deviance .smaller}

- **Type I:** each term after the terms written before it
- **Type II:** each main effect after the other main effects; an interaction after the mains
- **Type III:** each term after every other term, including interactions

The three answer different questions. Pick one before fitting, and do not use Type I unless the order is the scientific order.

For a generalised linear model the same partition is an analysis of deviance. The statistic is a likelihood-ratio $\chi^2$, or a score test, rather than an $F$ on residual sums of squares. `anova(glm(...), test = "LRT")` is that comparison of nested models. It is still a test of a term in a model, not a new model. His 2025 notes put the conditional mean, the probability, the quantile, and the hazard on one page as the functions that comparison can target.

::: {.notes}
Type I, II, III definitions are different questions—pick before fitting. GLM partition is analysis of deviance with LRT, not $F$ on SS. His 2025 note bundles mean, probability, quantile, hazard as comparison targets—one line, do not over-read.
:::
## Favour the model, not a pretest

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.8
flowchart LR
  question["Question"]
  support["Support of $$Y$$"]
  family["$$Y \mid x \sim \mathrm{family}(\mu)$$"]
  check["Residual plot"]
  report["Estimate and interval"]
  question --> support --> family --> check --> report
```

A pretest that switches you from a $t$-test to a rank test still does not estimate $\mu = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$. Rank tests answer a different contrast, and they have assumptions of their own.

The teaching sequence for the three models follows the SIB day on logistic regression and GLMs ([slides](https://github.com/sib-swiss/advanced-statistics/blob/master/docs/assets/pdf/Day2-LogisticregressionandGLM-2026.pdf), [course](https://www.sib.swiss/training/course/20260907_ADDMG)).

::: {.notes}
Walk the Mermaid: question → support → family → residual plot → estimate. Pretest switching $t$ to ranks still misses $\mu$. SIB day link is for students who want the full logistic/GLM course—optional aside.
:::
## Two names, one role each {#sec-lm-names}

[Angelino and Marcone](https://www.sib.swiss/training/course/20260907_ADDMG) (SIB, Lausanne, September 2026) use two roles. The **response**, also called the dependent variable, is what the model describes or predicts. That is \(Y\) on the [notation](#sec-notation) slide.

The **explanatory variable** is also called an independent variable, a predictor, or a covariate. That is \(x\). The question picks it. The general line is \(Y = f(x) + \text{error}\). A function \(g(Y)\) on the left is a transformed response, which is the case the [previous slides](#sec-log-estimand) treat as a change of estimand.

::: {.notes}
Response $Y$ versus explanatory $x$; $g(Y)$ on the left is the transformed-response case from earlier. Angelino and Marcone SIB attribution. Link notation slide if someone asks for $\mathbf{x}$.
:::
## The formula is the model {#sec-lm-formula}

In R the same line is `response ~ predictors`. Read `~` as "described by".

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} `+` adds a term. `-` or `-1` drops one, including the intercept.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} `:` is an interaction. `*` is the interaction and the main effects. `^n` adds interactions up to degree \(n\).

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} `I()` is arithmetic. `age^2` in a formula is not \(age^2\). The square is `I(age^2)`.

`y ~ 1` is the null model: the mean, and no covariate. One mixed formula example is `Income ~ age^2 + I(weight/height^2) + gender`.

::: {.notes}
Step fragments: `+`/`-`, `:`/`*`/`^n`, `I()` for arithmetic. `y~1` is intercept-only. `age^2` in a formula is not squared age—`I(age^2)` is. Mixed example at the bottom is one sentence.
:::
## One row, then every row {#sec-lm-matrix}

For one observation,

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_{p-1} x_{i,p-1} + \varepsilon_i.
$$

Stacked, that is \(\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\). The first column of \(\mathbf{X}\) is 1 when the model has an intercept. Least squares chooses \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) to minimise the sum of squared vertical residuals. The fitted values are \(\hat{\mathbf{Y}} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{Y}\), and \(\mathbf{H}\) is the [hat matrix](#sec-hat).

::: {.notes}
Display $Y_i=\beta_0+\cdots+\varepsilon_i$, then $\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$. $\hat{\mathbf{Y}}=\mathbf{H}\mathbf{Y}$ introduces the hat matrix for leverage later.
:::
## Ordinary least squares is BLUE {#sec-gauss-markov}

The [Gauss–Markov theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Markov_theorem): if \(\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i) = 0\), the \(\varepsilon_i\) are uncorrelated, each has the same finite variance \(\sigma^2\), and \(\mathbf{X}\) has full column rank, then

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}
$$

has the smallest variance among linear unbiased estimators. The errors do not have to be Gaussian for that result. Gauss used normality. Markov removed it.

If, in addition, the \(\varepsilon_i\) are independent and Gaussian, that same \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is the maximum-likelihood estimator. The \(t\) tests and the \(F\) test on the printout use this extra assumption. If the variances differ or the errors are correlated, the corresponding estimator is generalised least squares, which is the [Welch case](#sec-ols-replacements) when the variance is a group.

::: {.notes}
Gauss–Markov needs zero mean, uncorrelated equal-variance errors, full-rank $\mathbf{X}$—not Gaussian errors for BLUE. Gaussianity enters for MLE and for $t$/ $F$ on the printout. GLS is named when variance differs.
:::
## A coefficient is a \(t\) {#sec-lm-t}

`summary(lm)` tests each coefficient against 0. The statistic is the estimate divided by its standard error. [Angelino and Marcone](https://www.sib.swiss/training/course/20260907_ADDMG) note that this test assumes Gaussian residuals. It is the interesting test for a slope. It is rarely the question for the intercept.

In a model with several covariates, each line is the test of that coefficient **with the other terms already in the model**. [Mahanty](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/interpreting-linear-model-output-r-anil-mahanty/) (9 January 2018) maps the same printout. Two of his readings do not travel: multiple \(R\) is not a count of points on the line, and a small \(p\) is not a verdict that the model fits.

::: {.notes}
Each `summary(lm)` line tests that coefficient with others already in. Mahanty's two warnings: multiple $R$ is not a point count; small $p$ is not goodness of fit. Intercept $t$ is rarely the scientific question.
:::
## The \(F\) test compares two nested models {#sec-lm-f}

The \(F\) statistic on the same printout compares the fitted model with the intercept-only model. The statistic is the drop in the residual sum of squares, per extra parameter, divided by the remaining residual mean square:

$$
\frac{\{\mathrm{SS}(\mathrm{mean}) - \mathrm{SS}(\mathrm{fit})\}/(p_{\mathrm{fit}} - p_{\mathrm{mean}})}{\mathrm{SS}(\mathrm{fit})/(n - p_{\mathrm{fit}})}.
$$

With a single slope, this \(F\) matches the \(t\) test of that slope. With several slopes, every coefficient can be quiet and the \(F\) test can still reject. \(R^2\) is the share of the variance of \(Y\) that the fit captures. Adjusted \(R^2\) charges a cost for each extra term. The residual degrees of freedom are \(n\) minus the number of estimated parameters.

::: {.notes}
Read the $F$ ratio formula once; with one slope it matches slope $t$. Several quiet slopes can still yield a significant $F$. $R^2$ and adjusted $R^2$ definitions are on the slide—df is $n$ minus parameter count.
:::
## A factor shifts the intercept {#sec-lm-ancova}

The height example is `Height ~ Age + Gender`. Gender is a factor, so R codes it as an indicator against a reference level. Women are the baseline in the printout. The line for women is \(124.52 + 2.72\,\mathrm{Age}\). The line for men has the same slope and a higher intercept, \(127.3 + 2.72\,\mathrm{Age}\).

That is an analysis of covariance: one continuous covariate, one categorical factor, and a common slope unless you add `Age:Gender`. The gender coefficient is a difference of intercepts, not the raw difference of the two mean heights. The sums of squares for that fit still depend on [which ANOVA type](#sec-anova-type) you ask for.

::: {.notes}
`Height~Age+Gender`: women $124.52+2.72\,\mathrm{Age}$, men same slope, higher intercept $127.3$. Gender coefficient is intercept difference, not raw mean difference. ANOVA type still matters for SS.
:::
## Four plots, then two more {#sec-lm-plot}

`plot()` on an `lm` draws four checks by default: residuals against fitted values, a normal QQ plot, scale against location, and residuals against leverage ([`plot.lm`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/versions/3.6.2/topics/plot.lm)). Those are `which = c(1, 2, 3, 5)`.

[Tay](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2019/11/the-hidden-diagnostic-plots-for-the-lm-object/) (14 November 2019) notes the two that are not in that panel. `which = 4` is Cook's distance against the row number. `which = 6` is Cook's distance against leverage over one minus leverage. He treats a Cook's distance above 1 as a point to inspect. The next four slides are the default four, each with a fit that respects the assumption and a fit that does not. Illustrative draws, seed `20261005`.

::: {.notes}
Default `plot(lm)` is which 1,2,3,5; Tay adds Cook vs index (4) and Cook vs leverage (6). Cook $>1$ to inspect. Next four slides are the default panel, seed 20261005 illustrative fits.
:::
## Residuals against the fitted values

![Two residual-versus-fitted plots. Left: a flat cloud around zero. Right: a U-shape from fitting a straight line to a quadratic.](figures/generated/lm-resid-fitted.png){fig-alt="Left, residuals from a straight-line fit sit in a flat band around zero. Right, residuals from a straight line fitted to a quadratic curve form a U." width="96%"}

A flat cloud is the linear mean. A curve means \(f(x)\) is still in the residual.

::: {.notes}
Left panel flat cloud is the linear mean assumption; right U-shape is missing curvature in $f(x)$. Pair with the smoothing section later. This is the first of four diagnostic figures—code was on the prior slide.
:::
## The residual QQ plot

![Two normal QQ plots of residuals. Left: points along the line. Right: heavy tails from a t distribution.](figures/generated/lm-qq.png){fig-alt="Left, Gaussian residuals follow the normal reference line. Right, residuals from a heavy-tailed draw flare at both ends." width="92%"}

Same reading as the [shape figures](#sec-qq-shapes). A line supports the Gaussian assumption behind the \(t\) and \(F\) tests. A flare is a heavy tail, and the next slide changes the model for \(Y\).

::: {.notes}
Gaussian residuals on the line; $t$ residuals flare both tails. Same vocabulary as the opening QQ shapes. Flare here motivates changing the family for $Y$, not only the mean structure.
:::
## Scale against location {#sec-lm-scale-location}

![Two scale-location plots. Left: a flat smooth of the square-root absolute residual. Right: the smooth rises because the variance grows with x.](figures/generated/lm-scale-location.png){fig-alt="Left, the square root of the absolute residual stays level across fitted values. Right, it rises as the fitted value increases." width="96%"}

A flat smooth is constant variance, the Gauss–Markov condition. A rise is a variance that travels with the mean: [generalised least squares](#sec-ols-replacements), or a family in which the variance depends on \(\mu\).

::: {.notes}
Flat smooth of $\sqrt{|\text{residual}|}$ is constant variance; rising smooth is variance with mean. Link to $\phi V(\mu)$ in GLMs and to GLS on the replacements slide.
:::
## Leverage and Cook's distance

![Two residual-versus-leverage plots. Left: points near the origin, inside the Cook contours. Right: one point far to the right with a large residual.](figures/generated/lm-leverage.png){fig-alt="Left, residuals sit at small leverage. Right, one observation has high leverage and a large residual, beyond a Cook's-distance contour." width="96%"}

Leverage \(h_{ii}\) is the diagonal of the hat matrix. A common cut is \(2p/n\) or \(3p/n\) from Belsley, Kuh, and Welsch (1980). The contours are Cook's distance 0.5 and 1.

::: {.notes}
Leverage $h_{ii}$ from the hat matrix; cuts $2p/n$ or $3p/n$ from BKW. Cook contours 0.5 and 1 on the figure. High leverage plus large residual is the point to name on the right panel.
:::
## The link acts on $\mu$, not on $Y$ {#sec-glm-link-mean}

Agresti writes a generalised linear model as one object: a distribution for $Y$, a linear predictor, and a link on the conditional mean [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015].

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Link on the mean**

::: model
$$
g(\mu_i) = \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}
$$
:::

After the fit, $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid \mathbf{x}) = g^{-1}(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta})$ is a probability, an expected count, or a positive rate.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Transform of $Y$**

$$
g(Y_i) = \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \varepsilon_i
$$

That sentence rewrites each observation before the fit. It targets $\mathbb{E}\{g(Y)\}$, which is not $g(\mu)$ when $g$ is nonlinear.
:::
::::

The [estimand slides](#sec-log-estimand) are what the second column costs.

::: {.notes}
Left column: $g(\mu_i)=\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}$. Right column transforms each $Y_i$ and targets $\mathbb{E}\{g(Y)\}$. Walk both callouts; estimand slides are the cost of the right column.
:::
## $E\{g(Y)\}$ is not $g\{E(Y)\}$ {#sec-glm-jensen}

For a nonlinear $g$,

$$
\mathbb{E}\{g(Y) \mid \mathbf{x}\} \ne g\{\mathbb{E}(Y \mid \mathbf{x})\}.
$$

Regressing $\log Y$ targets $\mathbb{E}(\log Y \mid \mathbf{x})$. A log link targets $g(\mu) = \log \mu$. In general $\exp\{\mathbb{E}(\log Y \mid \mathbf{x})\} \ne \mathbb{E}(Y \mid \mathbf{x})$. A transformation model and a log-link GLM are different sentences about $Y$.

::: {.notes}
Display the inequality for nonlinear $g$. $\log Y$ regression versus $\log\mu$ link are different sentences—repeat the exp of mean log versus mean example from earlier if needed.
:::
## The family matches the type of $Y$ {#sec-glm-family-match}

Ordinary least squares on a transformed response still carries a Gaussian error on whatever scale you chose.

A GLM keeps $Y$ on its support and changes the family:

- Bernoulli or binomial for a 0/1 outcome or a proportion
- Poisson for a non-negative integer count
- Gaussian on the identity link when that support is appropriate

The [family table](#sec-family-table) is the first menu. The point here is that the likelihood is written for $Y$, not for $g(Y)$.

::: {.notes}
OLS on $g(Y)$ still assumes Gaussian errors on the transformed scale. GLM list: Bernoulli/binomial, Poisson, Gaussian identity. Likelihood is written for $Y$, not $g(Y)$—family table is next.
:::
## Variance travels with $\mu$ {#sec-glm-variance-mu}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Constant variance**

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma^2
$$

This is the classical linear-model assumption. A fan on [scale against location](#sec-lm-scale-location) is the picture that it has failed.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Variance tied to the mean**

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = \phi\, V(\mu_i)
$$

Poisson: $V(\mu) = \mu$. Binomial mean $\pi$: variance $\pi(1-\pi)$. The link is part of the family, not a fix applied to the residuals afterwards.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Left: $\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid x)=\sigma^2$. Right: $\phi V(\mu)$ with Poisson $V(\mu)=\mu$ and binomial $\pi(1-\pi)$. Fan on scale-location is the picture for the left column failing.
:::
## The link keeps $\mu$ in range {#sec-glm-link-range}

$\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}$ can be any real number. The inverse link maps it into the support of $\mu$.

- $\operatorname{logit}(\pi) = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}$ forces $0 < \pi < 1$
- $\log(\mu) = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}$ forces $\mu > 0$

A straight line on a transformed $Y$ does not give the same guarantee on the mean of the original response. That is why the [link stays on the mean](#sec-glm-versus-transform), not on $Y$.

::: {.notes}
Logit forces $0<\pi<1$; log link forces $\mu>0$. A line on $\log Y$ does not guarantee a valid mean on the original scale—inverse link does on $\mu$.
:::
## Coefficients read on the link scale {#sec-glm-coef-meaning}

The link is chosen so $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ answers a substantive question on the mean.

For $\log(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$,

$$
\frac{\mu(x+1)}{\mu(x)} = e^{\beta_1}.
$$

For a logit on $\pi$, $e^{\beta_1}$ is an odds ratio. The goal is not to make a histogram look Gaussian. The goal is a coefficient that names an effect on $\mu$. The compact contrast is [the link stays on the mean](#sec-glm-versus-transform).

::: {.notes}
For $\log\mu=\beta_0+\beta_1 x$, $\mu(x+1)/\mu(x)=e^{\beta_1}$. Logit: $e^{\beta_1}$ is an odds ratio. Goal is substantive effect on $\mu$, not a pretty histogram.
:::
## The response chooses the family {#sec-family-table}

| Support of $Y$ | A first model |
| --- | --- |
| Continuous, unrestricted, stable variance | Gaussian linear model |
| Two categories, truly binary | Logit, $Y \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi)$ |
| Non-negative integer, variance near the mean | Poisson, log link |
| Same, with extra-Poisson variance | Negative binomial, log link |

The next slides keep $\mu = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$ and change the family. A transformation of $Y$ is the other route, already set aside on the [estimand slides](#sec-log-estimand).

::: {.notes}
Table rows: continuous stable variance → Gaussian; binary → logit; count near equidispersion → Poisson; extra variance → negative binomial. Transformation route is explicitly set aside via log-estimand link.
:::
## The link stays on the mean {#sec-glm-versus-transform}

[Angelino and Marcone](https://www.sib.swiss/training/course/20260907_ADDMG) write the earlier models as $g(Y) = f(x) + \text{error}$. On a 0/1 response that line can return a probability below 0, because a straight line is not confined to $(0, 1)$.

In the generalised linear model the linearity sits on $g(\mu)$. The family then draws $Y$. The quantity you report is still a mean of the response you measured.

::: {.notes}
Angelino and Marcone: $g(Y)=f(x)+\text{error}$ on 0/1 can predict outside $(0,1)$. GLM linearises $g(\mu)$; family draws $Y$. Reported quantity remains mean of measured $Y$.
:::
## One skeleton for all three :link: {#sec-skeleton}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.4
flowchart LR
  fam["$$Y_i \mid x_i \sim \mathrm{family}(\mu_i)$$"]
  link["$$g(\mu_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$$"]
  mean["$$\mu_i = g^{-1}(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i)$$"]
  fam --> link --> mean
```

- **Family:** how $\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x)$ depends on $\mu$
- **Link** $g$: the scale on which $\beta_1 x$ is linear
- **Mean** $\mu = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$: what $\beta$ describes, after you invert $g$

Agresti is the reference for the theory and the worked models [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015]. Estimation is by maximum likelihood, not by a normal test of $Y$. The letters are fixed on the [notation](#sec-notation) slide.

::: {.notes}
Mermaid: family → link → $\mu=g^{-1}(\eta)$. Three bullets map to variance structure, scale of $\beta$, and mean after inversion. Agresti citation is the theory anchor; MLE not normal test on raw $Y$.
:::
## A continuous response, on the identity {#sec-glm-gaussian}

A continuous response goes to a linear regression. The drawing is Gaussian, and the link is the identity, so $\mu$ and the linear predictor are the same number.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.2
flowchart LR
  x["$$x$$"] --> eta["$$\eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$"]
  eta --> mu["$$\mu = \eta$$"]
  mu --> y["$$Y \mid x \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mu,\sigma^2)$$"]
```

::: {.notes}
Identity link: $\mu=\eta$. Mermaid ends at Normal$(\mu,\sigma^2)$. This is linear regression dressed in GLM notation—bridge for students who only know `lm`.
:::
## A binary response, on the logit {#sec-glm-bernoulli}

A binary response goes to a logistic regression. Here $\mu = \pi = \Pr(Y = 1 \mid x)$. The logit is the link used here. The probit is the alternative they mention later, and it stays close to this curve.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.2
flowchart LR
  x["$$x$$"] --> eta["$$\mathrm{logit}(\pi) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$"]
  eta --> pi["$$\pi = \mu$$"]
  pi --> y["$$Y \mid x \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi)$$"]
```

::: {.notes}
$\mu=\pi=\Pr(Y=1\mid x)$; logit link in the diagram. Probit mentioned as later alternative—stay on logit for odds-ratio reading.
:::
## A count, on the log {#sec-glm-poisson}

A count goes to a Poisson regression. The mean is often written as $\lambda$. That symbol is $\mu$ on these slides. The log link keeps $\mu > 0$, and $\exp(\beta_1)$ is a multiplicative change in the mean count.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.2
flowchart LR
  x["$$x$$"] --> eta["$$\log \mu = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$"]
  eta --> mu["$$\mu = \exp(\eta)$$"]
  mu --> y["$$Y \mid x \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)$$"]
```

Four working assumptions: $Y$ is a count per unit of time or space; $\log \mu$ is linear in $x$; the observations are independent; and $\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu$.

::: {.notes}
$\lambda$ on the slide is $\mu$ here; $\exp(\beta_1)$ multiplies mean count. Four assumptions at the bottom—especially $\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid x)=\mu$—are what CA-SYS will break.
:::
## The fit maximises the likelihood {#sec-glm-mle}

The fit is by maximum likelihood. For a Gaussian linear model that maximiser is the least-squares fit. For the logit and the Poisson log link there is no closed form: the estimates come from an iterative algorithm.

The Newton step for the logit, from the chapter embedded [below](#sec-burakov), uses the Bernoulli variances as weights:

$$
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t+1)} = \boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)} + (\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}^{(t)}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}(\mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol{\pi}^{(t)}),
\qquad w_i = \pi_i(1-\pi_i).
$$

::: {.notes}
The course notes state that the maximiser is iterative and do not write the update. The displayed step is Burakov's equation (2.87), in the chapter embedded later. $\mathbf{W}$ is diagonal. At convergence, $(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ is the estimated covariance of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$.
:::

## Hat values and Cook's distance, again {#sec-glm-influence}

The same two diagnostics carry over. Keep the hat-value cut at $2p/n$ or $3p/n$, the cut already used for the [linear model](#sec-lm-plot).

A Cook's distance above about $4/n$ is the cut in the [SIB notes](https://www.sib.swiss/training/course/20260907_ADDMG), and a Cook's distance above 1 is [Tay's](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2019/11/the-hidden-diagnostic-plots-for-the-lm-object/) cut for `plot(lm)`, also printed on the [checks figure](#sec-glm-checks): two sources, so quote the one you use.

::: {.notes}
Hat cut $2p/n$ or $3p/n$ as for `lm`. Say aloud that $4/n$ is the SIB cut and 1 is Tay's cut for `plot(lm)`; they are not two versions of one rule. Next slide is residual types.
:::
## Three residual scales {#sec-glm-resid}

Three residuals are worth plotting after a GLM.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} A deviance residual, plotted against the fitted value and against each covariate. A curve is a missing piece of the linear predictor.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} A Pearson residual, $(Y - \mu)$ divided by the fitted standard deviation. A trend against a covariate is a term the model does not yet contain.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} A quantile residual. Under the fitted family it is uniform on $(0,1)$. A QQ plot against normal quantiles is the picture. Extra-large tails are a signal to leave the Poisson for a quasi-Poisson or a negative binomial.

`acf()` is a quick check that the observations are not ordered in a way the independence assumption forbids. The Poisson simulation later draws the quantile residual for that family.

::: {.notes}
Step deviance, Pearson, quantile residuals and what curve each catches. Quantile residuals uniform under the fitted family—QQ against normal is the plot. `acf()` flags ordered dependence.
:::
## Two tiers of checks for a logit {.fit-fig #sec-glm-checks}

![Two tiers of logistic-regression checks: linearity of the log-odds, VIF, independence, Cook's distance; then separation, events per variable, and sparse categories.](figures/sources/logistic-model-checks.svg){fig-alt="Tier 1: a straight line on the log-odds scale, a VIF warning above 5 and a red flag above 10, independence as a design problem, and Cook's distance above 1. Tier 2: a zero cell and huge odds ratios, at least 10 events per variable as a rule of thumb that some recent work relaxes, and a category with no events to collapse." width="96%"}

The figure supplied with [this note](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7483052950236401665/). A bent log-odds line, a variance-inflation factor above 5, separation, and fewer than ten events per variable are the figure's warnings. Firth's penalised likelihood is the remedy it names for separation.

::: {.notes}
The LinkedIn post is behind a login wall, so the thresholds are the figure's own wording: VIF above 5 is a warning and above 10 a red flag; Cook's distance above 1 is a cause for concern; ten events per variable is a rule of thumb the figure says some recent work relaxes. Angelino and Marcone's Cook cut for a GLM is about $4/n$, stated on the previous influence slide.
:::

## Deviance is the residual sum of squares {#sec-glm-deviance}

Lack of fit is measured by the deviance. The null deviance $D_0$ compares the intercept-only model with the saturated model. The residual deviance $D$ compares the fitted model with the saturated model. Maximising the log-likelihood is the same operation as making $D$ small.

For nested models the likelihood-ratio statistic is the drop in deviance,

$$
D_{\text{small}} - D_{\text{large}} \sim \chi^2,
$$

with degrees of freedom equal to the number of extra parameters. In R that is `anova(model1, model2, test = "Chisq")`. This is the GLM form of the [analysis of deviance](#sec-deviance).

::: {.notes}
Their pseudo-$R^2$ is $1 - D/D_0$. They say that several pseudo-$R^2$ exist, and that a nested comparison should be the likelihood-ratio test. AIC is the comparison they allow when the models are not nested: deviance, plus a penalty for the number of parameters.
:::

## Quantile residuals check the family

These are randomised quantile residuals for a Poisson mean: if the family is right, they should look Gaussian. A heavy upper tail is a reason to leave the Poisson, not a reason to run Shapiro–Wilk on the raw counts.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
lower <- ifelse(y <= 0, 0, ppois(y - 1L, lambda = mu_hat))
upper <- ppois(y, lambda = mu_hat)
residual <- qnorm(runif(length(y), min = lower, max = upper))
```

::: {.notes}
Walk the code first: each count is spread uniformly over its step of the fitted distribution function, then mapped to the normal scale. The figure is on the next slide.
:::
## Quantile residuals check the family

![Two QQ plots of randomised Poisson quantile residuals. The Poisson sample tracks the reference line. The overdispersed sample lifts in the upper tail.](figures/generated/qq-quantile-residuals.png){fig-alt="QQ plots of randomised quantile residuals from a Poisson fit to Poisson counts and from a Poisson fit to overdispersed counts." width="96%"}

::: {.notes}
Walk the code, then the QQ plot. Stress that the reference is the fitted family, not marginal normality of the counts. Ask whether a heavy upper tail would change the variance model before they quote a rate ratio. About one minute.
:::

## Poisson · when the count matches the story {auto-animate=true}

Use it when $Y$ is a non-negative integer and, to a first approximation, $\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu$.

::: {data-id="pois-eq"}
$$
\log \mu = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x.
$$
:::

Colony counts on a plate are the clean case. Sequence reads are a count too, but with two complications: the sampling effort differs between samples, and the counts are more variable than a Poisson.

::: {.notes}
$\log\mu=\beta_0+\beta_1 x$ with data-id animate. Colony counts are clean; reads need offset and extra variance—foreshadow CA-SYS. Var equals mean is the assumption to test first.
:::
## Poisson · the CA-SYS version {auto-animate=true}

::: {data-id="pois-eq"}
$$
\log \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \mathrm{tilled}_i + \mathrm{year}_i + \log(\text{library size}_i).
$$
:::

$Y$ is the number of *Nitrospira* reads in a sample: a nitrite-oxidising genus, 153,771 reads across the 595 samples. The last term is the [offset](#sec-casys-offset), so $\beta_1$ is a ratio of rates per read.

::: {.notes}
Point out that the equation changed in two places from the previous slide: year entered as a factor, and the offset appeared. Neither is cosmetic. Without the offset, a sample sequenced twice as deeply looks twice as rich in Nitrospira.
:::

## Poisson · the call {#sec-casys-poisson-code}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
casys <- read.csv("data/derived/casys_teaching.csv")

fit_pois <- glm(
  nitrospira_reads ~ tillage + factor(year) + offset(log(total_reads)),
  family = poisson, data = casys
)

# Is one parameter doing both jobs?
sum(residuals(fit_pois, "pearson")^2) / fit_pois$df.residual
#> 10.6
```

A Poisson sets $\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu$. A Pearson statistic of 10.6 per degree of freedom says the data are about ten times more variable than that.

::: {.notes}
Run this if the laptop allows. The dispersion statistic is the number to look at before reading any coefficient, because the coefficient will look fine and the standard error will not. The rule of thumb is that a value near 1 is consistent with the Poisson; 10.6 is not a borderline case.
:::

## Negative binomial · same mean, one extra parameter {#sec-nb-theta}

Keep the log link. Add a dispersion parameter $\theta > 0$:

::: model
$$
\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu + \frac{\mu^2}{\theta}.
$$
:::

This is the `MASS::glm.nb` parameterisation: large $\theta$ means "close to Poisson". Agresti writes the same quadratic variance with a different symbol for the extra term [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015]. On these reads $\hat\theta = 29.3$.

::: {.notes}
Two readings of theta. Algebraically it is the inverse of the extra variance per unit of mean squared. Mechanistically it is a gamma-distributed latent rate, integrated out, which is the derivation on the Poisson-gamma slide. Stress that theta is not a second scientific effect to interpret.
:::

## One mean, two variance assumptions {#sec-casys-nb}

![Rate ratio for tilled against no-till, with a Poisson interval and a much wider negative binomial interval.](figures/generated/casys-poisson-vs-nb.png){fig-alt="Two horizontal intervals for the same rate ratio of about 0.97. The Poisson interval spans roughly 0.962 to 0.982; the negative binomial interval spans 0.941 to 1.002 and crosses one." width="94%"}

| Family | Rate ratio | 95% interval |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Poisson | 0.972 | 0.962 to 0.982 |
| Negative binomial | 0.971 | 0.941 to 1.002 |

::: {.notes}
This is the slide to slow down on. The point estimate barely moves, 0.972 against 0.971, because both models use the same mean equation. The interval is 3.1 times wider. Under the Poisson the contrast is "detected"; under the negative binomial it crosses one. Nothing about the biology changed between the two rows, only an assumption about the variance. Ask the room which interval they would put in a paper.
:::

## Read the mean, then $\theta$ {#sec-nb-read}

- []{.fragment fragment-index="1"} The rate ratio is a statement about $\mu$, on the log link, per read
- []{.fragment fragment-index="2"} $\theta$ is not a second effect; it describes leftover variation
- []{.fragment fragment-index="3"} A QQ plot of quantile residuals is the check, not a test that "selects NB"
- []{.fragment fragment-index="4"} With the wider interval, 1.00 is compatible with these data

A 2.9% lower rate under tillage would matter agronomically. These 595 samples cannot separate it from no difference.

::: {.notes}
The last line is the honest summary, and it is the pitfalls lesson applied to a real fit: the estimate is the result, and the interval says how much the data constrain it. Resist the temptation to call this a null finding. It is an imprecise estimate of a small contrast, which is a different sentence.
