:::

## The wrong family, on a QQ plot {#sec-casys-qq}

![Two QQ plots of residuals for the Nitrospira reads. The Gaussian linear model departs from the line at both ends; the negative binomial quantile residuals track it.](figures/generated/casys-qq-family.png){fig-alt="Left panel, standardised residuals from a Gaussian linear model on raw read counts, curving away from the reference line. Right panel, negative binomial quantile residuals close to the line." width="96%"}

::: {.notes}
Left is what you get if you put these counts into lm(). Right is the family the offset and the dispersion were chosen for. This is the same diagnostic as the earlier QQ slides, now on a real response rather than a draw, and it is the reason the family question comes before the test question.
:::

## Same count, three implementations

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Poisson

$$
\log \mu = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \log(\text{library size}), \qquad \mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu.
$$

Tilled against no-till: rate ratio **0.972** (0.962 to 0.982). Pearson $\chi^2/\mathrm{df} = 10.6$, so that interval is too narrow.

### Negative binomial

$$
\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta, \qquad \hat\theta = 29.3.
$$

Same mean equation: rate ratio **0.971** (0.941 to 1.002). The interval is 3.1 times wider and crosses 1.

### $\log(Y+1)$, then Gaussian

$$
\mathbb{E}\{\log(Y+1) \mid x\} = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}.
$$

That coefficient is not a rate ratio for $\mu$, and the library size no longer enters as an offset. The two means are not the same function of $x$.

:::

Arrow keys step the tabs. All three are fits to the CA-SYS reads, from `scripts/generate-data-figures.R`.

::: {.notes}
Tab through Poisson, NB, $\log(Y+1)$ Gaussian—arrow keys on slide. Rate ratio 0.972 vs 0.971, Pearson 10.6, $\hat\theta=29.3$, log-plus-one loses offset interpretation. Script path `generate-data-figures.R` if asked.
:::
## A count that is not Poisson {#sec-casys-richness}

![Observed richness by cropping system, in four yearly panels.](figures/generated/casys-richness-system.png){fig-alt="Boxplots with jittered points of observed OTU richness for systems SD1, SD2, TS1 and TS2, in panels for 2018 to 2021." width="96%"}

Richness is an integer, so the reflex is a Poisson. Pearson $\chi^2/\mathrm{df} = 27.8$ says otherwise: richness is a count of OTUs out of 10,633, bounded above and driven by sequencing effort.

::: {.notes}
A useful corrective. "Integer" does not imply "Poisson". Richness here is the number of distinct OTUs detected, so it is closer to a capture problem than to a rate: it is bounded by the reference table and it rises with library size. The honest teaching answer is that observed richness is a biased estimator of richness, and that the estimator belongs to the diversity literature rather than to a GLM slide. Note the 2018 panel is the pre-treatment baseline.
:::

## Detection depends on how hard you looked {#sec-casys-logit}

![Fitted logit curves for Methylobacter presence against standardised log library size, one curve per tillage class, with 0/1 observations jittered.](figures/generated/casys-logit-detection.png){fig-alt="Two rising logistic curves for probability of detecting Methylobacter against standardised log library size, with confidence ribbons and jittered binary observations." width="92%"}

*Methylobacter* is a methane oxidiser, present in 35% of samples. The odds of detecting it multiply by **1.74** per standard deviation of log library size.

::: {.notes}
This is the logit on a real response, and the result is uncomfortable in a useful way: the strongest predictor of presence is not a treatment, it is sequencing effort. The tillage odds ratio from the same fit is 1.34, with an interval of 0.95 to 1.91, so it is not separable from no effect here. Any presence-absence analysis of sequencing data has to carry library size, exactly as the count model carries the offset.
:::

## Equidispersion is one parameter doing two jobs {#sec-count-equi}

StatHarbor Analytics, *Count Data Models: From Poisson to Zero-Inflated Models*, starts from $Y \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)$ with $\mathbb{E}(Y) = \mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mu$. One rate controls the centre and the spread. The log link makes a one-unit step in $x_j$ multiply $\mu$ by $e^{\beta_j}$, a rate ratio.

The Poisson fit is the one they keep when the conditional mean is close to the conditional variance, the zeros are no more numerous than the Poisson predicts, and events are independent inside a fixed exposure. When $\mathrm{Var}(Y) > \mathbb{E}(Y)$, the same fit understates the standard errors. They name unobserved heterogeneity, omitted covariates, and clustering as the usual sources.

::: {.notes}
Poisson: $\mathbb{E}(Y)=\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu$; $e^{\beta_j}$ is rate ratio on log link. StatHarbor list when Poisson is OK versus when SEs are too small. Heterogeneity, omitted covariates, clustering as sources on the slide.
:::
## A gamma latent rate is a negative binomial {#sec-count-nb}

The same derivation gives the negative binomial as a Poisson–gamma compound: the Poisson rate is itself a gamma draw, and that draw is integrated out. The extra variance is unobserved heterogeneity.

$$
\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu + \frac{\mu^2}{\alpha}
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu + \alpha\mu^2.
$$

McCullagh and Nelder use the first form. The simulation slides call that shape $\theta$. In the second form, $\alpha \to 0$ returns the Poisson. Estimating $\alpha$ leaves the one-parameter exponential family.

::: {.notes}
Treating $\alpha$ as known keeps the model inside a one-parameter GLM. Estimating it is full maximum likelihood. StatHarbor reaches for the negative binomial when the variance exceeds the mean and the zeros come from the same process as the positive counts, and compares it with the Poisson by a likelihood-ratio test.
:::

## A point mass of zeros is a mixture {#sec-count-zip}

A zero-inflated model is a different generative story. With probability $\pi_0$ the observation is a structural zero. With probability $1-\pi_0$ it is a draw from a count distribution $f$. StatHarbor writes $\pi_0$ as $p$.

$$
\Pr(Y=0) = \pi_0 + (1-\pi_0)\,f(0),
\qquad
\Pr(Y=k>0) = (1-\pi_0)\,f(k).
$$

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.6
flowchart LR
  z["$$\pi_0$$"] --> zero["structural zero"]
  z --> count["$$1-\pi_0$$"]
  count --> f["$$f$$: Poisson or NB"]
  f --> y["$$Y$$"]
  zero --> y
```

A logit for $\pi_0$ plus a log-linear Poisson is the zero-inflated Poisson. The negative binomial in $f$ is the zero-inflated negative binomial. Neither is an exponential-family GLM.

::: {.notes}
StatHarbor compares a zero-inflated model with an ordinary Poisson by AIC, BIC, or a Vuong test, because those two models are not nested.
:::

## Four count models, three questions {#sec-count-table}

| Model | Extra variance | Structural zeros | Exponential family |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Poisson | No | No | Yes |
| Negative binomial | Yes | No | Only if the dispersion is fixed |
| Zero-inflated Poisson | No | Yes | No |
| Zero-inflated negative binomial | Yes | Yes | No |

The practical line under the table: diagnose dispersion and extra zeros before you quote a rate ratio. An ill-matched family understates the uncertainty.

::: {.notes}
Table: extra variance, structural zeros, exponential family column. Practical line under table—diagnose before quoting a rate ratio. ZIP and ZINB are not GLMs in the strict sense.
:::
## The count measures a latent share {#sec-measure}

[Sarkar and Stephens](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41588-021-00873-4) separate a measurement model from a model for the latent intensity. The paper is about genes in single cells. The same split applies to any feature counted inside a sample of finite depth: a taxon, a transcript, a fragment.

Let $s_i$ be the library size, the total count in sample $i$, and let $\lambda_{i\ell}$ be the relative intensity of feature $\ell$, a share of that sample. The measurement model is

$$
Y_{i\ell} \mid s_i, \lambda_{i\ell} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(s_i \lambda_{i\ell}).
$$

Dividing by the depth is this rate: the offset $\log s_i$, with its coefficient fixed at 1.

::: {.notes}
$Y_{i\ell}\mid s_i,\lambda_{i\ell}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(s_i\lambda_{i\ell})$; offset $\log s_i$ with coefficient 1. Sarkar–Stephens single-cell paper, same logic for any feature in finite depth.
:::
## The measurement drawing {#sec-measure-dag}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.4
flowchart LR
  lam["$$\lambda_{i\ell}$$"] --> rate["$$\mu_{i\ell}=s_i\lambda_{i\ell}$$"]
  s["$$s_i$$"] --> rate
  rate --> y["$$Y_{i\ell}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_{i\ell})$$"]
```

Library size and relative intensity meet in the Poisson mean. The Pearson-residual figure below is this regression, with the slope of $\log s_i$ fixed.

::: {.notes}
Mermaid: $\lambda$ and $s$ meet in $\mu=s\lambda$, then Poisson draw. Pearson-residual figure below is this regression with fixed log-depth slope.
:::
## Three assumptions in the measurement layer {#sec-box1}

Box 1 of Sarkar and Stephens lists the assumptions behind that Poisson measurement model.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} In each sample, each molecule is equally likely to be observed.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} Each molecule is observed independently of the others.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} Only a small proportion of the molecules present are observed. They cite 10–20% in a typical single-cell experiment.

Assumptions 2 and 3 are the ones they treat as plausible. Assumption 1 fails when stability, cellular location, or sequence changes the chance that a molecule is seen. A bias that is shared across samples can enter the Poisson model as a covariate. A bias that changes from sample to sample is extra noise, and the measurement model that carries it is negative binomial. If a later protocol observes a larger share of the molecules, the measurement variance falls relative to a Poisson.

::: {.notes}
Step fragments: equal capture probability (often fails), independence (plausible), small observed fraction 10–20% (plausible). Sample-specific bias → NB measurement model per slide text.
:::
## A zero is an observation {#sec-zeros}

Sarkar and Stephens refuse the phrase "missing data" for a zero count. The picture: a minute with no cars at an intersection is a zero; an hour when the observer is away is a missing record. A sequencing zero is the first of those. Imputing only the zeros treats them as holes.

They also drop the word "dropout" for a supposed device that writes a zero whatever the true intensity. Spike-in controls, in the papers they cite, did not support a zero-inflated *measurement* model. A zero-inflated *observation* model can still be the right margin when the latent intensity itself has a point mass at zero.

::: {.notes}
Cars-at-intersection versus absent observer—sequencing zero is the first. No impute-only-zeros; spike-in evidence against dropout measurement model. ZI on latent intensity can still be right.
:::
## The observation model is the margin {#sec-obs-model}

An expression model is a distribution $g_\ell$ for the latent share $\lambda_{i\ell}$. The observation model is the distribution of $Y$ after $\lambda$ has been integrated out.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.4
flowchart LR
  g["$$\lambda_{i\ell}\sim g_\ell$$"] --> poi["$$Y_{i\ell}\mid s_i,\lambda_{i\ell}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(s_i\lambda_{i\ell})$$"]
  poi --> marg["margin of $$Y_{i\ell}$$"]
```

A gamma $g_\ell$ produces a negative-binomial margin. A point-gamma $g_\ell$, a spike at zero plus a gamma, produces a zero-inflated negative-binomial margin. The Poisson recommendation is for the measurement layer. The margin is usually wider, because the latent share varies across samples.

::: {.notes}
$g_\ell$ for latent $\lambda$; integrate to margin of $Y$. Gamma → NB margin; point-gamma → ZINB. Poisson recommendation is measurement layer; margin usually wider.
:::
## One feature at a time {.smaller #sec-tbl-single}

| Latent model for $\lambda$ | Margin of $Y$ | Methods they name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Point mass | Poisson | Analytic |
| Gamma | Negative binomial | MASS, edgeR, DESeq2, SAVER, BASiCS |
| Point-gamma | Zero-inflated NB | PSCL |
| Unimodal, nonparametric | Unimodal | ashr |
| Point-exponential family | Flexible | DESCEND |
| Fully nonparametric | Flexible | ashr |

Table 1 of Sarkar and Stephens. Each row is a latent model for one feature, combined with the Poisson measurement model. The method column is the software they list for that margin.

::: {.notes}
Table 1 Sarkar–Stephens: latent model row drives margin and software column. Point mass → Poisson analytic; gamma → edgeR/DESeq2 class tools. One row per feature with Poisson measurement.
:::
## Several features together {#sec-tbl-multi}

| Link $h$ | Noise on the latent scale | Methods they name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identity | None | NMF, scHPF |
| Identity | Gamma | NBMF |
| Log | None | GLM-PCA |
| Log | Gamma | scNBMF, GLM-PCA |
| Log | Point-gamma | ZINB-WaVE |
| Neural network | Point-gamma | scVI, DCA |

Table 2. A multi-feature model writes the share through a low-rank factorisation and a link $h$, then adds a noise distribution for the stochastic piece. Overdispersion relative to the Poisson measurement changes the variance of $Y$ and leaves the mean of the structured part to be read with that measurement model in mind.

::: {.notes}
Table 2: link $h$, noise on latent scale, named methods. ZINB-WaVE and scVI are multivariate—not the single-feature GLM from earlier. Overdispersion changes $Y$ variance, mean read with measurement model.
:::
## Depth in the offset, dispersion in $\theta$ {.fit-fig #sec-pearson-nb}

![Negative binomial observation model: latent state and sequencing depth, an offset regression on depth, Pearson residuals, and a shrinkage of the dispersion across features.](figures/sources/pearson-residuals-nb.svg){fig-alt="Panel A: a negative binomial observation model whose variance is mu plus mu squared over theta, with a biological latent state and technical sequencing depth. Panel B: log mu equals a feature intercept plus log depth, slope fixed at 1, and residuals after that regression. Panel C: the Pearson residual divides the raw residual by the negative-binomial standard deviation. Panel D: a shrinkage of the per-feature dispersion toward a trend in the mean." width="98%"}

Read the gene labels as any feature. Depth is the offset. The quadratic term in $\theta_\ell$ is the extra variance.

::: {.notes}
Panel A: NB variance $\mu+\mu^2/\theta$ with biology and depth. B: offset regression; C: Pearson $r$; D: shrink $\hat\theta_\ell$. Gene labels stand in for any feature.
:::
## The Pearson residual for that fit

$$
\log \mu_{i\ell} = \beta_{0\ell} + \log s_i,
\qquad
r_{i\ell} = \frac{Y_{i\ell}-\mu_{i\ell}}{\sqrt{\mu_{i\ell}+\mu_{i\ell}^2/\theta_\ell}}.
$$

The coefficient of $\log s_i$ is fixed at 1. A Poisson model has no $\theta_\ell$, so the split between a latent intensity and a depth has a parameter in the negative binomial. The figure's last panel shrinks a noisy $\hat\theta_\ell$ toward a smooth of the mean.

::: {.notes}
Display $\log\mu_{i\ell}=\beta_{0\ell}+\log s_i$ and Pearson $r_{i\ell}$ formula. Coefficient on $\log s_i$ fixed at 1. Last panel shrinks noisy $\hat\theta_\ell$—split measurement from dispersion.
:::
## Condition on the total, or integrate a prior {.fit-fig #sec-count-map}

![A map of six count distributions: Poisson to negative binomial by a gamma prior; gamma to Dirichlet by normalising; Poisson to multinomial, and negative binomial to Dirichlet-multinomial, by conditioning on the sum.](figures/sources/count-distribution-connections.svg){fig-alt="Poisson with mean equal to variance; a gamma prior integrated out gives the negative binomial with variance mu plus mu squared over alpha; normalising independent gammas gives a Dirichlet; conditioning independent Poissons on their sum gives a multinomial; conditioning independent negative binomials on their sum gives a Dirichlet-multinomial. Gamma and Dirichlet are the continuous members." width="92%"}

[Townes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.04343). Vertical arrows condition on the sum. Horizontal arrows integrate a continuous prior. Gamma and Dirichlet are the continuous nodes.

::: {.notes}
Townes map: vertical condition on sum, horizontal integrate prior. Poisson→multinomial, NB→Dirichlet-multinomial; gamma↔Dirichlet. Continuous nodes are gamma and Dirichlet.
:::
## The first two moments, by the tower rule {#sec-tower}

Write the Poisson rate as a latent $\lambda$ with $\mathbb{E}(\lambda) = \mu$. The law of total expectation and the law of total variance give the margin without a new pmf:

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y) = \mathbb{E}\{\mathbb{E}(Y\mid\lambda)\} = \mu,
\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}(\lambda) + \mathrm{Var}(\lambda) = \mu + \mathrm{Var}(\lambda).
$$

::: {.notes}
Read $\mathbb{E}(Y)=\mu$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mu+\mathrm{Var}(\lambda)$ from the tower identities. No new pmf needed—variance inflation from latent $\lambda$.
:::
## Compound, mixture, and the Tweedie line

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} $\lambda$ fixed: $\mathrm{Var}(\lambda) = 0$, and $Y$ is Poisson.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} $\lambda$ continuous: a compound distribution. A gamma $\lambda$ is the negative binomial. A normal draw for $\log\lambda$ is the Poisson log-normal. Townes notes that this margin has a heavier tail than the negative binomial.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} The latent discrete: a mixture. The zero-inflated model is the spike at a structural zero plus a count distribution.

Townes's Poisson–Tweedie has $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mu + \phi\mu^{p}$. The negative binomial is $p = 2$. These margins generally have no closed likelihood.

::: {.notes}
Step three fragments: fixed $\lambda$ Poisson; continuous $\lambda$ compound (gamma NB, log-normal heavier tail); discrete latent mixture including ZIP. Tweedie $\mathrm{Var}=\mu+\phi\mu^p$, $p=2$ is NB; often no closed likelihood.
:::
## Independent counts, given their sum {#sec-multinomial-sum}

Townes's identity: independent Poisson counts, conditioned on their total, are one multinomial draw. If $Y_\ell \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_\ell)$ independently and $M = \sum Y_\ell$, then

$$
\mathbf{Y} \mid M \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}\!\left(M,\; \pi_\ell = \lambda_\ell \big/ \textstyle\sum_k \lambda_k\right).
$$

The same step with independent negative binomials that share a scale parameter returns a Dirichlet-multinomial. The shared scale is required. Negative binomials with a shared shape and different means do not, after conditioning, stay Dirichlet-multinomial.

A sequencing library is this conditioning. The Sarkar rate $s_i\lambda_{i\ell}$ is the Poisson layer. Given the library size, the vector of features is multinomial. Modelling the counts as independent Poissons with an offset, or as one multinomial, are the two sides of that identity.

::: {.notes}
Poisson conditioned on $M$ → multinomial with $\pi_\ell=\lambda_\ell/\sum\lambda$. NB with shared scale → Dirichlet-multinomial; differing shapes break that. Library size conditioning is the sequencing identity.
:::
## Logit · only if $Y$ is really binary {auto-animate=true}

Detection of a taxon in a core is binary. A flux cut at an arbitrary threshold is the dichotomisation we have already rejected.

::: {data-id="logit-eq"}
$$
\mu = \pi = \Pr(Y = 1 \mid x).
$$
:::

The mean of a 0/1 response **is** the probability.

::: {.notes}
$\mu=\pi=\Pr(Y=1\mid x)$; flux dichotomisation rejected. Mean of 0/1 is probability—say it plainly before the simulated pH slide.
:::
## Logit · a simulated detection {auto-animate=true}

$x$ is centred pH, from $-1.5$ to $1.5$. $Y$ is 1 if the taxon is detected.

::: {data-id="logit-eq"}
$$
\mathrm{logit}(\pi) = \log \frac{\pi}{1-\pi} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x.
$$
:::

Fitted here: $\hat\beta_0 = -0.32$, $\hat\beta_1 = 1.44$.

At $x = 0$, $\hat\pi = \mathrm{logit}^{-1}(-0.32) \approx 0.42$.

Same seed, same script, still not a field dataset.

::: {.notes}
$\hat\beta_0=-0.32$, $\hat\beta_1=1.44$; at $x=0$, $\hat\pi\approx 0.42$. Centred pH $-1.5$ to $1.5$; same seed script, not field data.
:::
## Logit · the curve is the result

The band is for $\pi$, not for a single core. A core is still 0 or 1.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
fit_bin <- glm(y_bin ~ ph, family = binomial)
pi <- plogis(predict(fit_bin, type = "link"))
```

::: {.notes}
Two lines: fit on the logit scale, back-transform with `plogis()`. The saved figure is on the next slide.
:::
## Logit · the curve is the result

![Logit curve of detection probability against centred pH, with jittered binary points and a band for the probability.](figures/generated/logit-fit.png){fig-alt="Binary detections against centred pH, with a fitted logit curve and a Wald band on the probability scale." width="84%"}

::: {.notes}
Stress that the band is for $\pi$, not for a single 0/1 core. The code slide is excerpt only; the figure is the saved fit. Ask the room to say the estimand in words before they quote $\exp(\beta_1)$. About one minute.
:::

## Logit · odds move by a factor, probabilities do not

A one-unit increase in centred pH multiplies the **odds** by

$$
\exp(\hat\beta_1) = 4.2
$$

Wald 95% interval: **2.4 to 7.4**.

In this fit, $\hat\pi$ goes from about **0.42** at $x = 0$ to about **0.75** at $x = 1$. That is a change of about 0.34 on the probability scale, not a 4.2-fold change in probability.

The interval is symmetric on the logit scale. It is not symmetric on the probability scale.

::: {.notes}
$\exp(\hat\beta_1)=4.2$, Wald interval 2.4 to 7.4 on odds scale. $\hat\pi$ about 0.42 to 0.75 is ~0.34 on probability scale—not a 4.2-fold change in $\pi$. Interval symmetric on logit, not on $\pi$.
:::
## The regression is for $\pi$ {#sec-logit-is-regression}

[Olszewski](https://medium.com/@r.clin.res/is-logistic-regression-a-regression-46dcce4945dd) places logistic regression in the generalised linear model: the target is a function of $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$. For a Bernoulli response that function is $\mathrm{logit}(\pi)$, and $\pi$ is the conditional mean. A classifier that thresholds $\pi$ is one use of the fitted probability.

He dates the logit to Berkson, as an alternative to the probit, and the unified GLM to Nelder and Wedderburn (1972, [their paper](http://www.medicine.mcgill.ca/epidemiology/hanley/bios601/Likelihood/NelderWedderburn1972.pdf)). In R the same statement is `glm(y ~ x, family = binomial(link = "logit"))`.

::: {.notes}
Olszewski: logistic regression targets $\mathrm{logit}(\pi)$; threshold classifier is one use. Berkson logit history and Nelder–Wedderburn GLM paper as on slide; R call `family=binomial(link="logit")`.
:::
## A test of two proportions is this model {#sec-proportion-tests}

In the [first of the two follow-ups](https://medium.com/@r.clin.res/testing-hypotheses-about-proportions-through-the-logistic-regression-and-friends-57f4b4a8d93c), the Wald statistic for a difference of two proportions, with unpooled variances, matches the average marginal effect of a logistic regression with one binary predictor. The sampling scheme is two independent binomials, without a small-sample correction. He calls the algebra a conceptual bridge: the statistics match, and the note does not re-prove the asymptotic distribution.

The [second note](https://medium.com/@r.clin.res/testing-hypotheses-about-proportions-through-the-logistic-regression-and-friends-part-ii-b917f48da6f3) matches the pooled two-proportion $z$, the statistic behind `prop.test()`, to the Rao score test of the same logistic model. Wald, score, and likelihood-ratio statistics agree asymptotically. The pooled statistic is the score test. Several grouping factors are an analysis of deviance for proportions, the GLM form of the [deviance partition](#sec-deviance). A numeric covariate beside the group is the [analysis-of-covariance](#sec-lm-ancova) analogue.

::: {.notes}
Part I: unpooled Wald matches logistic AME; part II: pooled `prop.test` matches Rao score. Several groups → deviance; numeric covariate → ANCOVA analogue links on slide.
:::
## The fitting criterion is cross-entropy {#sec-cross-entropy}

Denis Burakov, in the chapter embedded below, starts from Fisher's binomial likelihood and writes the average negative log-likelihood. For $y_i \in \{0,1\}$ and fitted probabilities $\hat\pi_i$,

$$
-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[y_i\log\hat\pi_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat\pi_i)\right].
$$

The factor $1/n$ does not move the maximiser. This is the log loss, also called cross-entropy. In his table, $y = 1$ and $\hat\pi = 0.19$ costs $-\log 0.19 = 1.66$; $\hat\pi = 0.79$ costs $0.23$. With an intercept in the model, the fitted probabilities add up to the number of observed events.

::: {.notes}
Burakov log loss: $-\frac1n\sum[y\log\hat\pi+(1-y)\log(1-\hat\pi)]$. Table row $\hat\pi=0.19$ costs 1.66 versus 0.79 costs 0.23. Intercept-only fitted probs sum to event count.
:::
## The logit, rather than the probit {#sec-logit-not-probit}

Burakov quotes Berkson's reasons for the logistic curve over the probit: a closed-form derivative, fits that on Berkson's data were as close as the probit or closer, and coefficients that exponentiate to odds ratios. A probit coefficient is a change in a standard normal deviate.

Angelino and Marcone add the complementary log-log link, $\log\{-\log(1-\pi)\} = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}$, for a curve that is asymmetric about $1/2$. They report that probit and complementary log-log fits are often close to the logit. The link on these slides stays the logit, so that $\beta_1$ remains a change in log odds.

::: {.notes}
Berkson reasons on slide: derivative, fit quality, odds ratios. Complementary log-log for asymmetry at 1/2—probit and cloglog often close to logit. Deck stays logit for $e^{\beta_1}$ reading.
:::
## One-hot coding is a contrast with a reference {#sec-one-hot}

Burakov's worked table has 700 borrowers, 100 defaults. High delinquency: 80 defaults out of 180. Low delinquency: 20 out of 520. The model is $\mathrm{logit}(\pi) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$, with $x = 1$ for high delinquency.

The intercept $\hat\beta_0 = -3.219$ is the log-odds in the reference group, a probability of $0.0385$. The slope $\hat\beta_1 = 2.996$ multiplies the odds by $e^{2.996} = 20$. One category is absorbed into the intercept. The coefficient is the contrast with that category.

::: {.notes}
700 borrowers, 100 defaults; high delinquency $\hat\beta_0=-3.219$ → $p=0.0385$; $\hat\beta_1=2.996$ → odds $\times 20$. One category absorbed into intercept.
:::
## Weight of evidence centres on the sample {#sec-woe}

Weight of evidence asks a different contrast with the same fit. The sample default rate is $100/700 = 0.1429$, and its logit is $-1.7918$. A category's weight of evidence is its own log-odds minus that overall logit.

The difference of the two weights equals the one-hot slope: $\Delta\mathrm{WOE} = 2.9957 = \hat\beta_1$. Subtracting a constant does not change a variance, so the standard error of a weight of evidence equals the standard error of that category's log-odds.

With a single categorical predictor the two codings describe one model. With several categorical predictors, Burakov notes that one-hot coefficients move when the reference level changes, while the weights of evidence stay centred on the overall event rate.

::: {.notes}
Overall default rate 100/700, logit $-1.7918$. $\Delta\mathrm{WOE}=2.9957=\hat\beta_1$. SE of WOE equals SE of category log-odds; with several factors, WOE stays centred when one-hot slopes move.
:::
## Softmax is the logit for $K$ classes {#sec-softmax}

For $K$ mutually exclusive classes, $\sum_k \pi_k = 1$, Burakov writes the softmax

$$
\Pr(Y = k \mid \mathbf{x})
  = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_j)}.
$$

Fixing $\boldsymbol{\beta}_K = \mathbf{0}$ leaves $K-1$ vectors. Estimating all $K$ is the unconstrained softmax. The probabilities match. $K = 2$ with a zero reference class is binary logistic regression.

::: {.notes}
Display softmax with $\boldsymbol{\beta}_K=\mathbf{0}$ identification. $K=2$ with zero reference recovers binary logit. Cross-entropy loss with 1-of-$K$ indicators on slide.
:::
## Softmax, drawn

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.2
flowchart LR
  x["$$\mathbf{x}$$"] --> scores["$$\eta_k=\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}_k$$"]
  scores --> sm["softmax"]
  sm --> pi["$$\pi_k$$"]
  pi --> y["$$Y\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$$"]
```

The class probabilities sum to 1. The cross-entropy is $-\sum_i\sum_k t_{ik}\log\pi_{ik}$, with $t_{ik}$ the 1-of-$K$ indicator.

::: {.notes}
Ordered categories are a cumulative model. Burakov notes them and stays with the unordered softmax.
:::

## The chapter, on this slide {#sec-burakov}

Denis Burakov, *Logistic Regression: From Maximum Likelihood to Machine Learning*, is the source of the loss, the weight-of-evidence arithmetic, and the softmax. The viewer scrolls the chapter.

{{< pdf references/burakov-logistic-regression.pdf width=100% height=500 >}}

::: {.notes}
Embedded PDF—students scroll Burakov for loss, WOE, softmax details. One sentence: this is reference material, not a live read-through. Keep timing short unless asked.
:::
## A Wald interval is a large-sample interval for $\pi$ {#sec-wald-pi}

Burakov builds the interval for a new covariate row $\mathbf{x}_0$ on the logit, then inverts it. The covariance of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is $(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}$, with $w_i = \hat\pi_i(1-\hat\pi_i)$.

$$
\mathbf{x}_0^{\top}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
  \pm 1.96\sqrt{\mathbf{x}_0^{\top}\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}})\,\mathbf{x}_0}.
$$

The endpoints are symmetric on the logit. After the inverse logit they sit inside $(0,1)$ and they are not symmetric on the probability scale. The justification is the asymptotic normality of the maximum-likelihood estimator. A small sample, or the perfect separation on the [checks figure](#sec-glm-checks), is outside that justification.

::: {.notes}
Build on logit with $(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}$; invert to $(0,1)$, asymmetric on $\pi$. Separation and small $n$ break asymptotics—link checks figure.
:::
## A conformal interval uses a calibration set {#sec-conformal}

The same chapter then builds an interval whose coverage is finite-sample, under exchangeability, from a calibration set that was not used to fit $\boldsymbol{\beta}$.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} Fit the logit on the training rows.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} On the calibration rows, score each residual. The Pearson form he uses is $(y - \hat\pi)/\sqrt{\hat\pi(1-\hat\pi)}$.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} Add and subtract a quantile of those scores. On the logit scale the interval is symmetric around $\mathrm{logit}(\hat\pi)$, and the inverse logit brings it back to $(0,1)$ without clipping.

A classical conformal prediction set for a binary label is a set of classes. The interval here is for $\pi$. Whether the 0/1 outcome falls inside a narrow band for $\pi$ is a different question, and he treats it as the wrong coverage check.

::: {.notes}
Step three fragments: train fit; calibration Pearson scores; symmetric band on logit then inverse logit. Coverage is for $\pi$, not for whether 0/1 falls in band—Burakov's distinction on slide.
:::
## Hold the other covariates still

With several covariates,

$$
g(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots
$$

$\exp(\beta_1)$ is the multiplicative change in the mean, or in the odds, for a one-unit step in $x_1$ **with the other covariates held at the same values**.

If $x_2$ is a mediator or a collider, "held still" is a different estimand, not a more adjusted one.

::: {.notes}
$\exp(\beta_1)$ with $x_2,\ldots$ fixed at chosen values. Mediator or collider makes "held still" a different estimand—not "more adjusted is always better".
:::
## Ad hoc, post hoc, intrinsic {#sec-hoc}

[Qin Ma](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-025-02852-0) uses the three words for bioinformatics, and they transfer. An ad hoc analysis answers one question with one pre-chosen tool. A post hoc analysis, in that paper, reconciles several tools or several datasets after the fact. An intrinsic analysis builds the check into the model.

In this workshop "post hoc" also means the comparisons you make after a model that has more than two levels. Those are not the same operation. The next slides are the second meaning. Choosing the comparison because it was the significant one is [data dredging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_dredging): the hypothesis was suggested by the same data that are asked to confirm it.

::: {.notes}
Ma's three words for omics; workshop "post hoc" also means planned contrasts after multi-level fit—disambiguate. Data dredging link when the contrast was suggested by the same data.
:::
## Contrasts from the model you fitted

When the groups and the covariates are in one model, the comparisons are contrasts from that fit. [Heiss](https://www.andrewheiss.com/blog/2022/05/20/marginalia/) separates two averages. An average marginal effect averages the contrast over the observed rows. A marginal effect at the mean evaluates it at the average covariate. `marginaleffects` defaults to the first. `emmeans` defaults to the second. They differ when the model is not linear.

Reporting several of those contrasts is still a family. The adjustment is simultaneous inference for the family you planned, not a correction chosen after the significant rows appear.

::: {.notes}
Heiss: average marginal effect versus effect at mean; `marginaleffects` vs `emmeans` defaults. Several contrasts still form a family needing simultaneous inference.
:::
## A row of coefficients is a family {#sec-multiplicity}

$$
H_{0j}: \beta_j = 0, \quad j = 1, \ldots, p.
$$

One row per coefficient hides that family. The matching statement is a joint region, or simultaneous intervals: Bonferroni intervals for a Bonferroni test, Tukey or Scheffé intervals for those contrast families. A logistic, Poisson, or negative-binomial model has the same family. The criterion does not change because the distribution did.

::: {.notes}
StatHarbor Analytics, *Multiple Testing Correction* (2026), from the slide "Multiplicity in Linear Models". Testing and interval estimation are dual: a family-wise procedure induces simultaneous intervals with joint coverage at least \(1-\alpha\). Pointwise bands on a curve are the individual-test object; a simultaneous band is the corrected one.
:::

## The follow-up matches the family

After a global analysis of variance, name the contrasts before you test them.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} All pairwise means: Tukey.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} Each treatment against a control: Dunnett.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} Arbitrary contrasts: Scheffé, or simultaneous inference from the fitted model.

The correction belongs to that family. It is not a fee paid because several means exist.

::: {.notes}
Tukey all pairs, Dunnett versus control, Scheffé arbitrary—match procedure to planned family. Correction is not a tariff for having many means.
:::
## Genomics is a large exploratory family

A screen of thousands of genes, tens of thousands of proteins, or millions of variants is a different family. Missing a true signal is costly, and a controlled share of false leads is acceptable.

That is a false-discovery rate: Benjamini–Hochberg, an adaptive version, or a \(q\)-value. A \(q\)-value is not a posterior probability that the finding is true. A family-wise guarantee of no false claim at all spends power the screen cannot afford.

::: {.notes}
Thousands of features: FDR (BH, adaptive, $q$-value) not FWER. $q$ is not posterior probability of truth—power trade-off on slide.
:::
## One false claim, or some false signal

[]{.fragment fragment-index="1"} A family-wise error rate is the right target when even one false claim is costly.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="2"} A false-discovery rate is the right target when the aim is broad discovery and some controlled false signal is acceptable.

[]{.fragment fragment-index="3"} Dependence, a hierarchy, or a structured set of contrasts often recovers power that a generic worst-case correction spends.

A procedure that controls the family-wise rate also controls the false-discovery rate, usually at that cost in power.

::: {.notes}
Because \(V \le R\) whenever \(R > 0\), the false-discovery rate is at most the family-wise error rate. Holm rejects every hypothesis Bonferroni rejects, for the same family and the same level. Questions before choosing: what is the family, is the setting confirmatory or exploratory, what false-positive burden is tolerable, and are the tests independent, positively dependent, or structured? Report the family, the criterion, the procedure, and the adjusted summary. Do not choose the correction after seeing which rows were small.
:::

## Which procedure for which family

| Scenario | Family | Typical procedure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary confirmatory endpoints | Small and prespecified | Holm, gatekeeping, closed testing |
| All pairwise means | Structured contrasts | Tukey HSD |
| Many genomic features | Very large, exploratory | Benjamini–Hochberg, adaptive BH, \(q\)-values |
| Complex dependence | Structured and correlated | Westfall–Young, or a bootstrap calibration |

Define the family and the error criterion before the claims. This grid is from StatHarbor Analytics, *Multiple Testing Correction* (2026).

::: {.notes}
Walk the table: confirmatory Holm/gatekeeping; pairwise Tukey; genomics BH; dependence Westfall–Young or bootstrap. StatHarbor 2026 grid—define family before claims.
:::
## Two places to go next

[@bretzMultipleComparisonsUsing2016a] develops these procedures as maximum statistics and shows the R implementations. [@farcomeniReviewModernMultiple2008] reviews the false-discovery proportion, dependence among the statistics, and the genomic case.

::: {.notes}
Bretz multiple comparisons book for R implementations; Farcomeni review for FDR and dependence. Bibliography slide—thirty seconds unless someone asks for a recommendation.
:::
## A table of counts is a log-linear model {#sec-loglinear}

[Penn State STAT 504, Lesson 10](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/Lesson10) models a contingency table by a Poisson GLM. The cell count is $Y_{ab} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_{ab})$. The lesson is this log-linear model. Independence, with neither margin as the response, is

$$
\log \mu_{ab} = \alpha + \alpha_a + \alpha_b.
$$

::: {.notes}
$Y_{ab}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_{ab})$; independence $\log\mu_{ab}=\alpha+\alpha_a+\alpha_b$. PSU STAT 504 lesson—joint model, not logit of one margin.
:::
## Independence, drawn

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.2
flowchart LR
  a["level $$a$$"] --> eta["$$\log\mu_{ab}=\alpha+\alpha_a+\alpha_b$$"]
  b["level $$b$$"] --> eta
  eta --> y["$$Y_{ab}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_{ab})$$"]
```

The fitted counts are row total times column total over $n$, and every odds ratio equals 1. A logit model is the conditional distribution of one margin. This log-linear model is the joint distribution. Dummy coding changes the separate coefficients. Differences of coefficients, the log odds, stay put.

::: {.notes}
A logit-equivalent log-linear model includes every association among the predictors. The lesson contrasts R's dummy coding, first level set to 0, with the zero-sum constraint in `loglin()`. Expected counts do not depend on that choice.
:::

## A normal latent on the log mean {.fit-fig #sec-pln}

![The Poisson log-normal model: counts and covariates enter a latent Gaussian layer, the counts are Poisson given the latent, and the same layer is constrained for a known grouping, a mixture, a low-rank covariance, or a sparse precision.](figures/sources/poisson-log-normal.webp){fig-alt="Standard Poisson log-normal. Counts Y and covariates X enter a latent Z drawn normal with mean mu and covariance Sigma. Given Z, the counts are Poisson with mean exp of Z. The mean of Z is X times a coefficient matrix. Extensions constrain that mean for known classes or unknown groups, and constrain Sigma to low rank or to a sparse precision." width="96%"}

[Chiquet, Mariadassou, and Robin](https://doi.org/10.3389/fevo.2021.588292). The figure's $\mu$ is the mean of the latent Gaussian. Here that mean is $m$, and $\mu$ stays $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$.

::: {.notes}
Chiquet figure: latent $Z$, Poisson on $\exp(Z)$, extensions constrain $\mathbf{m}$ or $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. Figure $\mu$ is latent mean $m$; slide $\mu$ stays $\mathbb{E}(Y\mid x)$.
:::
## The Poisson log-normal drawing

$$
\mathbf{Z}_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\mathbf{m}_i, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}),
\quad
m_{i\ell} = \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\theta}_\ell,
\quad
Y_{i\ell}\mid Z_{i\ell} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\!\left(\exp(o_{i\ell}+Z_{i\ell})\right).
$$

Townes: replace the gamma prior on the rate by a log-normal. The normal is the distribution of $\log$ of the Poisson mean.

::: {.notes}
Read $\mathbf{Z}_i\sim\mathrm{Normal}(\mathbf{m}_i,\boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ and Poisson on $\exp(o+Z)$. Townes: log-normal latent replaces gamma for rate.
:::
## The moments sit above the Poisson line {#sec-pln-moments}

Aitchison and Ho, as quoted by Chiquet, Mariadassou, and Robin, give the margin after integrating the latent:

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y_{i\ell}) = \exp\!\left(o_{i\ell} + m_{i\ell} + \sigma_{\ell\ell}/2\right),
$$

$$
\mathrm{Var}(Y_{i\ell}) = \mathbb{E}(Y_{i\ell}) + \mathbb{E}(Y_{i\ell})^2\left(e^{\sigma_{\ell\ell}}-1\right).
$$

The variance exceeds the mean. The covariance of two features has the sign of $\sigma_{\ell\ell'}$. Given $\mathbf{Z}_i$, the features are independent, so the dependence lives in $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. Twice the effort adds $\log 2$ to the offset $o_{i\ell}$.

::: {.notes}
The likelihood has no closed form once $\mathbf{Z}$ is integrated out. The paper fits it by a variational approximation, in the R package `PLNmodels`. The four corners of the figure constrain either $\mathbf{m}$ (a known class, or a mixture) or $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ (low rank, or a sparse precision).
:::

## What these three models do not cover

- a zero-inflated count is the [mixture](#sec-count-zip) already named, and it sits outside the exponential family
- a composition is the [conditioning on the library size](#sec-multinomial-sum); a log-ratio, after a deliberate treatment of the zeros, is a further model
- a continuous flux: often a positive continuous distribution, or a Gaussian model on a scale you can defend
- dependence in space or in time: the design block is next

Quasi-Poisson is a variance fix, not a full likelihood. Use it only if you can say what the interval means.

::: {.notes}
Bullet list: ZI mixture, composition conditioning, continuous flux, space-time design next. Quasi-Poisson variance fix only if you can interpret the interval—closing honesty slide.
:::
